speechtext: That in accordance with the recommendation contained in the 19th report of the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders, that portion of the 49th rule which limits the time for receiving petitions for private Bills he suspended in reference to the petition of the New Brunswick Southern Railway Company, presented this day, praying for an Act to declare their railway to be for the general advantage of Canada, and that the said petition be read and received forthwith.

I would like to understand the reason why this particular measure demands a suspension of the rules of the House'. I have not heard any reasons given thus far. The hon. gentleman who is making the motion will no doubt be able to inform the House.

The petition was handed to me by the Southern Railway Company of New Brunswick. The reason they come here is that the Hon. Mr. Blair, the chairman of the Railway Commission, told the'm that the legislation which they had obtained from the provincial legislature of New Brunswick was not sufficient, and that they should obtain legislation from the Dominion parliament. I only received the petition the day before yesterday.

I have not been able to gather from the hon. gentleman's statement why the rules of the House should be suspended in favour of this petition. If he is not able to give any reason, perhaps he would give us an opportunity to examine the petition. The mere fact that somebody has written a letter to the railway company does not seem to afford a sufficient reason why the rules of the House should be suspended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that the reason given by my hon. friend is this, that this legislation was passed by the legislature of New Brunswick, but that in order that it should have the effect intended, it is necessary for the company to have a Dominion charter. I understand that the company were informed only recently that their charter was insufficient for their purposes, and that they would have to obtain the necessary powers from this parliament. That is the only reason.

If that is the reason, it is not set forth in the petition, and I do not understand on what principle this petition has received the favourable report of the committee to which it was referred.

The petition sets out that legislation is desired from this parliament for two purposes. One is to confirm two Acts of the legislature of the province of New Brunswick relating to the company, passed in 1901 and in 1902. Therefore, so far as they are concerned, there has been abundant opportunity to have this Bill introduced within the proper time. That portion of the petition affords not the slightest ground for a suspension of the rules of this House, if they mean anything. If they mean nothing, but if we can set them aside on the most trivial pretexts, as we have been doing during the last six weeks, let us abolish them altogether. If they do mean something, let us require, both in this House and in the committees of this House, some better reason than that stated in this petition. If the suspension of the rules of this House is to be a mere form, let us understand it at once. The second purpose stated in the petition is to construct a bridge over the St. Croix river, in the province of New Brunswick, at the terminus of the company's railway. The petition recites :
That the company was incorporated under the said chapter 74 of the statutes of 1901 of New Brunswick, with power to acquire the Shore Line Railway, and the deed of transfer was confirmed by the said chapter 102 of the statutes of 1903.
That is all that there is in this petition, which I understand has been reported favourably by a committee of this House. What the committee found in that petition to report favourably upon I do not know. If the rules of the House are to be observed, I think this Bill ought not to be received under the facts set forth in the petition. I am not for one moment stating that this will not be desirable legislation. It may be legislation that I myself would support. All I am calling attention to is that we are deliberately, day after day, and week after week, violating the rules of this House on the flimsiest possible pretexts, and in this case without any pretext at all. All I am suggesting is that we should adopt some course that would be reasonable

either abolish the rules of the House or, if they require to be suspended, let that suspension be based on some reason that is worthy of the name.
I would like to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that this is not the preliminary petition. This petition does not state the reasons for delay. The other petition probably would.
I asked if the petition sets forth the reason and I asked it because my hon. friend did not give any. Perhaps my right hon. friend knows what are the reasons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know nothing more than I have said, but I understood the reason simply was that the chairman
of the Railway Commission had stated that their charter was insufficient and would have to be ratified by this parliament.

I have just had a few words from the hou. gentleman who introduced the Bill, and I have learned from him that it was only within a week that they became informed of the construction placed upon their charter by the Railway Commission. There can be no question of taking the public by surprise because another legislature had granted certain powers, and it is now discovered that these powers are not sufficient and will have to emanate from this House.

I have not suggested that the company were taking the public by surprise, but what I say is that we have a rule requiring that these Bills shall come before parliament within a certain time, and for a very good reason. The reason is that if they are not brought before parliament within proper time, they may not receive the consideration they should. I would like this to stand until I observe whether or not the preliminary petition sets forth any sufficient reasons why we should set aside the rules.
I only received the petition on Friday after the House had voted and have taken the first occasion to present it.

If there even was an occasion when the rule should be suspended it seems to me this is one. The company obtained legislation from the New Brunswick legislature. Then very recently they made application to the Railway Commission for power to construct a bridge in order to make connection at the Boundary river between Maine and New Brunswick with the Washington County Railway. They were told that their charter did not give them the right to make such an application and that it would be necessary for them to seek power from the Dominion parliament. They only learned this within the last week.
. It seems to me we ought not to enforce too rigidly our rules. Parliament is here for the purpose of serving the people, and here is a great public interest to be served.

Do I understand my hon. friend to say that the New Brunswick legislature had granted this company the right to build a bridge across the inter, national boundary or river which separates Canada from the United States ?

No. But the legisla-' ture gave power to connect with the Washington County Railway at the boundary. * Under that legislation, the company applied c to the Railway Commission, under the impression that the powers granted them by - the New Brunswick legislature were suffi-1 eient. The Railway Commission decided l against that view.
And rightly too.
Yes, very properly. Now they seek a remedy. They want to make the connection. It is in the public interest that connection should be made. Why should we hesitate to give the power ?

Surely the hou. gentleman is not so obtuse as to understand that we are objecting to the legislation. I distinctly said that I might very probably support the legislation, but I object to suspend the rules of parliament without any reason being stated. Parliament is, of course, the servant of the people, but it has to be governed by certain rules, and these rules should not be suspended without some plausible reasons being given. My hon. friend the Postmaster General says that this was only discovered recently. Assuming that to be the case, it ought to have been stated by the hon. gentleman who makes the motion.
So long as the House is informed of the reason, that ought to be sufficient.
It had not been stated to the House when I made my objection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, it was.
I did not hear it. When was this discovered ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend stated, when he introduced this petition, that this legislation was asked for because of the information given by the chairman of the Railway Commission that the powers vested in the company by the local legislature were inadequate.

The hon. Minister of Railways says that the Railway Commission very properly gave its information that the company had not the power to do what it was seeking to do. Then there must have been gross negligence on the part of the company. The company should have known that it had not that power.
Motion agreed to.

I would call the attention of the government, and especially of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) to an incident related in the Montreal newspapers. I refer particularly to ' Le Canada, ' but I think the same facts are stated in the other newspapers of Saturday last. If the statement of the facts is accurate, it would appear that the captain of a merchantman from Nova Scotia, Captain Taylor, while calling at a port in the Argentine Republic, was ordered by the British Consul to haul down the flag, the red ensign bearing the coat of arms of Canada. On his coming to Canada he has made public the fact. I would like to know since when a Canadian merchantman is not entitled to fly the Canadian flag. I do not call upon the minister to give an answer now, but I would be glad if he would ascertain the facts. I may remind the House that a number of years ago-in the seventies, I think-an Order in Council was adopted by the British government, upon the recommendation of the Lords of the Admiralty, allowing all vessels registered in Canada, belonging to the Canadian fleet, to use the red ensign with the Canadian coat of arms. And this was subsequently ratified by an Order in Council in Canada. So, if the facts of the case to which I have called attention are accurately given, it would appear that this British consul has not only insulted the loyal colony of Canada, but he has violated a direct order of the King adopted in England and in Canada. I hope the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see to it that justice is done In the matter.

The Inn,

Mr. George Taylor, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.

The motion referred to by Mr. Day in his letter is as follows :-

Permits or licenses for fishing in Canadian waters for 1904 can be procured from the undersigned at his office, Market Square, Kingston (one block from Folger's wharf). Office hours, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Ontario fishery overseer. Kingston, May, 1904.
This notice, it is evident, has been distributed all along the American frontier. It is taken by Americans to mean : You cannot drop a hook in Canadian waters unless you first go to Kingston and on one of the three special days in the week, between the hours of ten and four, attend a certain office and apply and pay for a license. Yet, it has been understood that the waters between Kingston and Ogdensburg were free to American anglers. And now Americans will not come over to our side, owing to the bungling with regard to fishing licenses between this government and the Ontario government.
I will send the notice and the letter to the minister, so that he may see definitely what is complained of and may issue some statement that can be given to our American friends to assure them that they are safe in coming to the Canadian side to spend their money, and fish in the river St. Lawrence.

It is clear to me that this notice was issued by the Ontario government, because we have no official of that name in our employ. I will communicate with the fishery commissioner of Ontario and see what I can do.

FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) I have an amendment to propose .to give the right of appeal to the Crown and not take it away from the subject. The question arises as to whether it would not be proper to let both parties have an equal right to appeal, subject to the limitation with respect to cost and securities. At present that right does not lie except in cases where the sum exceeds $500.
I have come to the conclusion that as this amendment is an important one so far as the Crown is concerned, that it is important that we should have the right to appeal, I am willing, in order to meet the objections made by the leader of the opposition, to broaden the right of appeal so as to give it to both parties. I therefore move to amend clause 1 by striking out the words in the 10th line ' on behalf of the Crown,'
Does that mean that in any case, however small, the amount may be the subject of an appeal to the Supreme Court ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what it means.

Surely that is going very far, it will subject private litigants to enormous cost. Now does that mean, for instance, that where a party has obtained an order for a commission to examine witnesses in another country, there shall lie an appeal on that order from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This will not apply to my hon. friend's case.

I am not speaking about a case in which I am interested. At the same time, it seems to me this is going very far, and it is against the spirit of our legislation, at all events, in the province of Quebec, where judgments, interlocutory in their nature, are not appealable except to certain specified cases. Let me put this case to my hon. friend ; here is a litigant who gets a decree for a commission to examine witnesses say in England, and the Crown wishes to appeal from this judgment or decree to the Supreme Court of Canada.

Everybody knows what it costs for such an appeal and I do not think it is fair or just that a litigant should be subjected to such a large amount of costs on a question which could be remedied by a final judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the matter could be remedied by a final judgment. It is in the interest of the Crown as well as of the individual that we should have an opportunity of settling as far as possible the jurisprudence and practice of tbe Exchequer Court. Cases are constantly rising in which it is important in the public interest that the Crown should have the right to have a principle settled, as for instance, in a small case, but on which a large amount may ultimately depend. For example, there was recently a case near Cornwall. on the judgment in which 40 or 50 cases depended, and it is important in the interest of the litigants that the principles applicable should be finally settled by the Supreme Court, and I do not think it is fair to assume, no matter who the Minister of Justice may be. whether it be my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) or any person else, that the Crown would undertake to advise appeals in eases where they would not be required in the public interest. But there may be exceptional cases in which such an appeal ought to be taken. Speaking from my own experience recently, I do not think of a single case in which there was a possibility of such an appeal as my hon. friend now says might arise.

Does my hon. friend think it would be well to limit the cases in which such an appeal could be taken to certain specified cases, as for instance cases which are enumerated in the code of civil procedure of Quebec. I do not know the practice in other provinces or whether in other provinces there lies an appeal to courts of appeal from any interlocutory or preparatory judgment in the lower court, but it seems to me it would be a hardship to litigants to have the law say that there would be an appeal from any interlocutory judgment rendered in a case. It might happen that in years to come the Minister of Justice might not be such a fair minded and judicial gentleman as the gentleman who occupies the position to-day and that under these circumstances probably litigants would not get such fair treatment as under other circumstances. I suggest that the law as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure of the province of Quebec be followed in this instance.
Section as amended, agreed to, and Bill as amended reported.
This is a matter of (procedure. I think that if my hon. friend does not specify in the Act that this law shall not apply to pending cases it will apply to them.

Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved second reading of Bill (No. 102) to amend the Shipping Casualties Act, 1901.
Does the hon. gentleman propose to explain this ?

This Bill is rather important. If it passes, the Act respecting inquiries and investigations into shipping casualties, assented to on the 23rd of May, 1901, and giving authority to an officer appointed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries "to examine into the case of a boat or ship which is stranded, will authorize him to investigate the case of the pilot. By section 4 of the Shipping Casualties Act the minister may direct the principal officer of customs residing at or near the place where the shipping casualty occurred, to hold an investigation ; but that investigation at present applies only to mates and engineers ; it does not apply to pilots. Sometimes, in order to satisfy the shipping interest, it would be necessai-y at the same time to examine into the case of the pilot, and it is proposed by this Bill to give the commisr sioner that power. I should think there would be no objection to the Bill. The Shipping Casualties Act was passed at the instance of the shipping interest some years ago, and on the special recommendation of the shipping interest on the other side of the water ; and anything that is done to satisfy the shipping people and the insurance companies that we are taking every precaution to protect the shipping interest is I think in the proper direction. That is why this Bill is introduced. There are other features in the Bill. For instance, the old by-laws of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners provided that the pilot's license should be suspended if an accident occurred to any vessel while in charge of a pilot until the cause has been investigated by the commissioners. This was manifestly unfair, because the pilots may not necessarily have been to blame, and was repealed. New subsection 2 of section 4 provides that if the officer holding the formal inquiry finds the pilot guilty of any of the offences enumerated, such officer may suspend the pilot's license until the minister decides whether a formal investigation is necessary. It is provided in the new Bill that the pilot must be
notified within three days that such formal investigation is to take place, otherwise his license could not be suspended. New section 27 provides that pilots may be dealt with under the Shipping Casualties Act in the same manner that masters, mates and engineers are, with the addition that pilots may be fined in lieu of suspension at the discretion of the court. This latter provision is extremely necessary, since, if a pilot) has caused the stranding, damage, collision, &c., of or to any vessel, it is generally through insufficient knowledge of the channel, and, by suspending such pilot, he is rendered more incompetent than before, whereas if a fine is instituted equivalent to his loss through suspension, the pilot s means of living are not taken away, and he has every opportunity to make himself more proficient in the knowledge of his pilotage duties.
Did the hon. gentleman say by whom that document was prepared ?

This is a report from the chairman of the examiners specially charged with this part of the business in my department. New section 28 provides against a pilot being tried by the harbour commissioners, Montreal Pilotage Court or pilotage authority of any district, after the case has been taken up under the Shipping Casualties Act. That means that he will not be tried twice for the same offence.

Will the hon. gentleman tell me whether this Act is to precede the pilotage Act, in the sense that the tribunal which is created here will take the place of the pilotage authorities in any district for the trial of pilots ?

In the case of a formal investigation, it would, because it says that if a formal investigation has taken place, and the case of the pilot has been tried, he cannot be tried a second time for the same offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Like my hon. friend opposite, I am somewhat interested in this Bill, and I think it means this, that in the case of a shipping casualty, an investigation may be ordered by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, in which case it is not held by the pilotage authorities, but by an authority appointed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. In that case the investigating officer may inquire into the responsibility for the casualty of any person connected with the boat, except the pilot. He has no authority to interfere with the pilot. The object of the Bill is to extend the power of that investigating officer to every person connected with the vessel, including the pilot ; and where the pilot's conduct may be part of the investigation, it is provided that no investigation may afterwards be made by the pilotage authorities. That is

the object of the last section. So that on the whole the only change is with respect to the authority that makes the investigation. Under the Pilotage Act the pilot would be subject to investigation by the pilotage authorities ; but this investigation, is held under the Shipping Casualties Act, and it seems perfectly fair that all persons responsible for the management of a vessel during the time the accident happened, should be subject to the same investigation.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Is it the intention to place the ' Stanley ' on the route between Summerside and Cape Traverse for the next season ? Last year she was taken off suddenly to Georgetown and Pictou, after having been only a few days on the route.

The ' Stanley ' was taken off the route between Summerside and Cape Tormentine when the season became too dangerous. There was so much ice that it would have been dangerous to leave the boat on that route. Instructions had been given to Captain Brown and Captain Far-quharson to use their own judgment in the matter, to join forces and put the two steamers on the same route as soon as the ice formed between Summerside and Cape Tormentine, and also between Pictou and Charlottetown. They were left to use their own judgment in the matter. Although this last winter was the most severe we have had for the last thirty or forty years, I think the ferry was kept in better shape than it ever was before. These two captains knew the route perfectly well, and when they saw there was danger they put on the two steamers between Georgetown and Pictou, and the result .was that navigation was suspended only for seven or eight days, instead of for weeks and months as in former winters.

As we are dealing with expenditure, I would like to ask the hon. minister what is the cause of the increased expenditure from 1896 to 1903 of $877,860.28. I notice that in the year 1896 the expenditure of the Marine and Fisheries Department wasi $793,634.49, and in the year 1903 it was $1,671,494.77. I believe it is due to the House and the country that the hon. minister should give! some explanation of this.

The explanation is clear from the blue-book. More steamers have been put in the service of both the Fisheries Department and the Marine Department ; the expenditure on aids to navigation is being increased year by year as the country develops ; and in the coming years it will have to be increased still further to satisfy the demands of the shipping interest and those interested in the fisheries. It is a well known fact that at the present time we cannot give to the shipping interests all they ask, in the way of permanent lights, improved fog alarms,, gas buoys, and other modern improvements. If the hon. gentleman looks at the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for 1903, he will see that from 1867 to the present date the expenditure has been increasing year by year on account of the development of the country.

What the hon. gentleman is quoting now, I suppose, forms part of the material that will in future years be considered part of the history of his administration-I mean his pamphlet. This pamphlet, to which we had occasion to refer the other evening, bears the signature of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and it is of very recent date-the 1st of February, 1904. The other evening the question came up why the hon. gentleman had selected the year 1896. This is the reason ho gave on that occasion :
It is alter 1896 that the most important work was done. In 1894-5-6, there were great complaints against the St. Lawrence route and we had any amount ol difficulty in dispelling the wrong impression that had been formed regarding it. We all know the efforts that were made by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and the shipping interests of Quebec and Montreal in 1896 to convince the government that it was a question of life or death for the St. Lawrence route that certain improvements should be made ; and it has been since that time that large sums were voted

in order to improve the route and remove the bad impression which had been formed concerning it.
When the hon. gentleman made that explanation, he had not borne in mind what appears on page 16 of his pamphlet. It is by a stretch of great courtesy that we call this a pamphlet; on the previous occasion it was called a campaign sheet. Here is what it says, under the heading ' Investigation into Causes of Casualties in the St. Lawrence ' :
Owing to misrepresentations , concerning this great waterway, to and from the sea, and ignorance of the causes which led to several casualties of ocean-going steamers, investigations have been held. The result shows that the casualties were not due to lack of effective aids to navigation, nor dangers existing in the river, but in nearly every instance, to some oversight or neglect on the part of those in charge for the time being. Several investigations have been held by the Imperial Board of Trade, and the confirmation of the above statement is found in the fact that several masters holding imperial certificates have been suspended.
The pilotage system of the past has been defective, and this question is now receiving attention with a view of introducing a more complete and effective system.
The other evening the hon. gentleman told us that it was because of complaints of a very serious character that large sums of money had to be spent ; and he tells us in his own pamphlet, prepared in his own department, and dated no longer ago than the 1st of February of the present year, that this was practically all a fiction-that it was not due to the want of aid, but to misrepresentation of the facts. I would like the hon. gentleman to reconcile these two statements if he can. They have both gone out to the public.
I think they agree perfectly.

The result shows that the casualties were not due to the lack of effective aids to navigation. The hon. gentleman declared the other night that the reason he selected 1896 to date the the improvements from, was because of the lack of effective aids to navigation, but he certainly has no ground on which to base any such argument.

In 1881 the expenditure in the Marine Department was $761,730.62. In 1896 it was-$793,,632.49, and in 1893 it reached $1,671,494.70, considerable over double. I would also draw attention to the fact that the cost of running the government steamers in Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia in 1888 amounted to $150,659.16. In 1896 it was only ?$145,315.29 and in, 1903 it amounted to
$363,813.97. I think .the hon. minister should explain this.
That is very easy to explain. In some years we buy boats and in others we do not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That does not appear in the Auditor General's Report.

Mr.-CASGRAIN. What about this steamer ' Gauss ' just come over ?
That was not a regular expenditure of the department, but for a special expedition to Hudson Bay. It was a special expenditure for the general account of three departments.
What department ?

The Department of the Interior, the Mounted Police and the Marine Departments. It is a special vote which was granted last year for this expedition, and we had to provide for a relief boat to remain in Hudson Bay. That is why we bought the ' Gauss.'
I understand that this expenditure is to be borne by the Department of the Interior, the Privy Council, which has the control of the Northwest Mounted Police, and the Marine Department ?

A special vote was asked and an amount of money was put at the disposal of the Marine Department to organize the expedition. The expedition is not for the benefit of the Marine Department particularly. We were only asked to carry out the preliminaries.
Is the expedition under the direct supervision of the Marine Department ?
Part of it is. The organization of the crew is, but not the whole of it. because a certain number of officials were furnished by the two other departments.
What price was paid for the ' Gauss ' ?

$70,000. The price was $75,000 if the boat went seven knots an hour and $70,000 if it did not. It did not go the seven knots an hour, so we paid $70,000. It is a new boat which was built for the German government three years ago for an exploration and it cost $155,000.
Has the difficulty between the late owners and the government been settled? We read in the papers that the boat was held at the port of departure foil the sum of $5,000.
I am not aware of the difficulty between the late owners and the government. I communicated with Mr. Bopp, the German consul at Montreal, and there was no difficulty.
Who chose the crew?

It was chosen by Captain Bernier himself and Captain Spain was authorized to examine the men with Captain Bernier before engaging them. Those who were found fit to go as sailors or officers were accepted.
Had Captain Bernier a free hand ?
I left him perfectly free to choose the best men, and for greater security Captain Spain was present at the choice.
I understand that there was a gunner who was sent over as one of the members of the crew. Had this boat any guns?
This man was not shipped as a gunner. The newspapers were evidently making fun. The name of the man was LaferriSre.
What occupation did he follow before he became a master gunner ?
I do not know
Is it true he was a reporter on one of the newspapers ?
Would that disqualify him ? If his physique was good and he fulfilled the conditions, I do not see where the disqualification would come in.

There is no disqualification, but it is a little strange that a newspaper reporter should be taken aboard the steamer [DOT] Gauss, ' not only as a member of the crew, but as a master gunner. There were no guns on the ship. It was not said jestingly that this was why this man,was taken aboard and paid by the government, but it was said in all truth and seriousness- he was taken on as a master gunner. There were no guns aboard, but even had there been, the man was absolutely unfit for the work he was appointed to do. He was there simply as a reporter for a certain newspaper in Montreal, but was shipped nominally as a master gunner in order that he might have a trip to Germany and back. If there is any truth in this I would like to know it. If the minister can deny it let him do so.
I read the report in the newspaper. It was all news to me, and I know nothing about it.
Is Captain Bernier still in the employ of the government ?
Yes, he is in charge of the ship.
Where ?
In Quebec.
Is the crew that brought the ship across still with the ship ?
No, they have all been discharged except those that are absolutely necessary while the boat is being repaired.
I suppose this crew was sent over for the special purpose of bringing the ' Gauss '[DOT] to Canada and not to take her to any special waters, as, for instance, to Hudson Bay ?
That is correct. And the whole crew was not sent from this side. There were only a few of the men, because we took some of the special officers, such as engineers from Germany.
How many were sent from this side ?
Sixteen.
And how many were taken from the other side ?
Six.

There seems to have been a great difference of opinion between the minister and Captain Bernier about the hiring of these men. I do not wish to misunderstand the minister. Do I understand him to say that these men were wholly and solely hired by Captain Bernier and that there was no interference with his choice ?

If I were to say 1 yes, ' in answer to that it would not be right. The master of the ship is under control of the department that hires him. In this case Captain Bernier was offered a list of a certain number of men and was called upon to make his choice from that list. And he was assisted by Captain Spain in making his choice. If he wanted to refuse any of the men, he could say so, and that man would be passed by.
I find in the Toronto ' Mail and Empire ' of 15th June, the following interview with Captain Bernier -

I have positive information from Captain Bernier over his own signature that he never gave any interview to any newspaper. Any interview that may be published as having come from him is made out of whole cloth.

This interview was published on June 15. It seems rather odd that

Captain Bernier has not contradicted it public-ally in the press. Perhaps the minister has not seen it.
Captain Bernier has had no time to contradict all that is said about him.

He has had a whole week. This interview is dated Quebec, and says
Capt. Bernier, who arrived here yesterday with his Arctic vessel, the ' Gauss,' after a thirty-six days' cruising, is far from satisfied with the personnel of his crew.
The ship does not seem over-speedy when she takes thirty-six days to cross the Atlantic.
He claims that with the exception of four men, including his first and second officers, the crew of twenty-four was foisted upon him by the Dominion government.
They were not of my choice, and, with the exception of a few good men, all land-lubbers or fresh water sailors who never went aloft in their lives or knew how to read a compass.
Some, no doubt, thought that because the [DOT] Gauss ' was a government vessel they were going on a pic-nic, but the moment we started from Bremerhaven I gave them to understand that I was master of the vessel. Nevertheless, they were unfit to work.
I stipulated with the government before leaving Canada that I required six men for each watch, but I found when we set sail that I could only have three ; the others were of no use. Consequently my officers and myself had to do double duty, and I was on the bridge the whole of every day until we came to anchor in the port of Quebec.
Among the crew as gunner was a young man named Laferri6re, who X have since learned is connected with a Montreal French paper. I do not know why he was given to me because the ' GaUss ' has no guns on board and in consequence was not in want of a gunner ;- but I presume influence was responsible for his appointment. X also had a steward who was forced on me, though I objected to him and who had the furnishing of the meat to the crew.
With regard to the complaints made about the quality of the provisions, Captain Bernier said :
Lord Dundonald completely in the shade. I am surprised that the minister allows his dignity to be offended by his subordinate in this fashion. Surely he is going to have Captain Bernier walk the carpet after this statement of his. I ask him again if any of the statements contained in the interview are correct ? .

I have no statement except the one I have just referred to.
I have, over the signature of Capt. Bernier a full denial of what has been put in the paper. And the report to me is perfectly satisfactory. I am not going to run to all the newspaper offices to tell them that Captain Bernier did not give an interview when I have his formal denial over his own signature. If I had the least doubt about the matter I would investigate. But I have no doubt. Captain Bernier knows his duty too well to have forgotten himself to the extent that has been mentioned. I believe that the report he has made to me is a faithful, a loyal and an honest report, and I have no other report to be guided by. If the newspapers take it upon themselves to make interviews, that is their own affair, I am not going to answer and I am not going to ask Captain Bernier to engage in correspondence. He is not a newspaper man. He has a fair education, but it is not his business to answer newspaper reports.
I think it would be only fair to Captain Bernier to have his report or letter go side by side with this intervfew. Will the minister lay it before the House ?
The report of Captain Bernier I can place before the House if it is required. It is an official l'eport, regularly filed. I will lay it before the House.
Is it a full denial of what is in the ' Mail and Empire ' ?
He says he never gave an interview to any newspaper.
The hon. minister first said it was a letter, and now he says it is a report. Which is it, a letter or a report ?

We will not. quarrel about the word, it is a report in the form of a letter if you like.
The provisions consisted of salt pork, hams, salt beef, sea-biscuit and flour. They wanted fresh bread, and you can judge for yourself what kind of sailors they were when they refused biscuits. I have sailed the ocean for thirty-five years as a master and in all my experience never heard of such a crew, and in future I will have the shipping of my own men or know the reason why.
Now, that interview was published on June 15, and it appears incredible that it should be wholly inaccurate in view of the fact that Captain Bernier has never denied it. Why, Captain Bernier has put

That is not the question at all. When we brought this matter up my hon. friend said it was a letter. Now a letter is supposed to be a public document, especially where it concerns an interview in a paper where the man denies ever having given the interview. Now the hon. gentleman is asked to produce this letter, which could be produced immediately before this committee. He says that it is part of a report which he will lay upon the table of the House. I ask the hon. gentleman to produce this document. I call his attention also to this fact which he has just

stated. He has just stated that Captain Bernier is not going to answer newspaper reports. But I may point out that when this interview was given in the ' Mail,' Captain Bernier was answering a report that bad appeared in the papers, and was also answering reports which had been given to the newspapers by some of the crew who complained bitterly of the treatment they had received on board that ship. So it was he that was answering these reports in the newspapers. When my hon. friend says that he is not going to ask Captain Bernier to answer in his report, he is beside the book, because this was given in answer to a report in a newspaper. Has my hon. friend read the reports in the ' Mail and Empire ? ' Has he not seen these interviews which were given by some members of the crew ?

If the other reports given to the newspapers are as truthful as the one which was put into the mouth of Captain Bernier, I do not think we need spend much time over them.
Mr. CASGRAlN. That may be my hon. friend's opinion, it is not ours. This is an important subject, it has been engaging the attention of newspapers in the city of Quebec and the city of Montreal ever since the ' Gauss ' arrived. Now I think it is due to Captain Bernier that whatever reproaches have been heaped upon him by the crew and other interested parties, should be cleared up. and got rid of. I know Captain Bernier well, and have known him for a long time. I formerly appointed him to a very important post, in which he gave the most complete satisfaction. From this post he was dismissed without any cause or reason whatever. The witnesses who were called against him testified that there never was such a good officer in the position he occupied as Captain Bernier. Now he has been accused publicly by these people, and amongst others, I believe, by this man La-ferri&re, of having brutally treated his crew, of having given them rations that could not be eaten, of having in other ways conducted himself not as a mariner, not as a master of a ship, but as a savage. I say it is in the interest of Captain Bernier, and it is only fair to him that these accusations should be cleared up, that these two accusations which have been brought against him should be disproved, and the proof should be given to this committee now in this discussion, so that the newspapers of the country which contained these reports may also contain the justification of Captain Bernier. This is the reason why I ask my hon. friend to produce this report, or his letter from Captain Bernier, so that we may get to the bottom of this matter which has attracted so much attention by the public ever since the 'Gauss arrived at Quebec.
What is the gross tonnage of the ' Gauss ? '
780 tons.
How is she propelled, by steam or by sail ?
By both.
What was her rate of speed across the Atlantic ?
I have not got the exact report yet, because Captain Spain has been away. Besides that, Captain Bernier was not in a hurry, and the weather was very bad during the passage.
Who was the officer who purchased the ship on behalf of the government 1

The details of the purchase are all contained in the department here at Ottawa. Captain Bernier himself was acquainted with the ship and recommended her strongly. Before closing the bargain we had her examined in Bremer-haven by Captain Mooney, who was superintending the construction of the ' Canada ' which was launched on the 14th of this month. He was commissioned to proceed to Bremerhaven and examine this boat thoroughly and make a report. It was he who informed us that the boat was not very fast and it was with that knowledge that we made a bargain with the Consul General at Montreal to be completed by Lord Strath-cona in London directly with the German government.
Would the minister state what is the horse-power of the boat ?
I could not tell that from memory. The vessel is not supposed to be altogether a steam vessel.

I understood the minister to state that Captain Bernier was presented with a list of persons from whom he was to choose his crew. Was the exact number of men on the list presented to the captain or was there a larger number ?
He was given a list of those who had made application for positions on the vessel, Some of them were chosen in Quebec and some in Montreal.
Were they all recommended ?
Captain Spain was instructed not to engage any man unless he was approved by Captain Bernier.
Was Captain Bernier at liberty to reject any of the men ?
At perfect liberty.
Did he have instructions to that effect ?
Captain Spain had instructions and I gave instructions personally to Captain Bernier.
That he might select whom he pleased ?
That he might select whom he pleased provided they had passed the necessary examination to which they were subjected by Captain Spain.

Now we are getting new light. Capt. Bernier was instructed to select from those who were recommended to him. I am endeavouring to find out whether he was perfectly free to ignore the list that was sent to him by the hon. gentleman. I would like to have a statement from the hon. gentleman whether Capt. Bernier was confined to those persons who were recommended to him by the department, I care not how good, if he had a free hand. If he was presented with a list and told that he might select from that list whom he pleased, that is not giving him a free hand. That is tying his hands entirely. I would like an explicit statement whether a list was submitted to Capt. Bernier from which he might alone select or if he was given permission to select outside of that list.

I have stated that twice already. A list of applicants was given to Capt. Spain and Capt Bernier and then there were a number of others who had applied to Capt Bernier directly and a certain number of students-I will call them students, although some of them were forty or fifty years of age-who frequented the naval school at Montreal, who were recommended to Capt. Bernier, by the director of the school at Montreal. Capt. Spain and Capt. Bernier went to Montreal and chose those whom they thought best qualified, but they were free to reject the whole list if they saw fit. They did the same thing at Quebec. The men with whom Capt. Bernier started were his own choice, and to me, the day he left for New York to take the steamer, he declared himself perfectly satisfied and made no complaint whatever. He makes no complaint at the present time and whatever the newspapers have published does not concern him because he has not thought proper to answer and it does not concern me at all. I have his report and am guided by that.
The explanation seems fair. The minister gave instructions to Capt. Spain.
Capt. Spain is responsible for the choice of the crew of any vessel under the department.

Were the instructions written ?
Mr. PREFONTAINE They might be, it was done in the department in the ordinary way. Some of the instructions were given verbally by myself.

We have at least the information that the ' Gauss ' has been
purchased in Germany and brought across the Atlantic and is now in Quebec. The result of her exploration we will know later. I would like to ask for information in regard to the ' Stanley.' I see an item here :
Baker, Ely & Co., Yarmouth, damage to wharf, caused by the ' Stanley ' colliding with the ' Prince Edward,' tearing her away from her moorings, $66.
How did that occur, who was in charge and why should she collide with the ' Prince Edward ' or tear away the wharf ?
Mr. PREFONTAINE I am informed it was a small matter, a mere accident, but I will furnish the details.
It may be small in the opinion of the hon. gentleman.
I am informed it is a small item and I will give the information.

I myself have further information. The hon. gentleman may think that when he pays a captain $100 a month to take charge of a steamship and then in addition to that the captain causes damage to the amount of $2,000 it is a very small matter to the people of this country. I assert in the interests of the people of this country that any damage in this way by a captain should cause his dismissal from the service. Has an investigation been held in this matter ?
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Has the minister got the information as to the accident that happened at Yarmouth between the ' Stanley ' and the ' Prince Edward ' ?

I have received this statement from my officers : the ' Stanley ' when going into Yarmouth harbour fouled the ' Prince Edward ' which was lying at the wharf. The tide was running out very strongly and the channel being very narrow, the 1 Stanley ' lost steerage way and in consequence came in contact with the ' Prince Edward ' and damaged her upper works. Mr. Stevens went to Yarmouth to assess the damages. The repairs were done by the Dominion Atlantic Company who own the ' Prince Edward,' and Mr. Stevens reported that the charges were reasonable. At Yarmouth the channel is so narrow, that with the strong current running the captain of the ' Stanley ' had a great difficulty in preventing his ship grounding. This happened about a year ago last May.
What was the total amount paid on account of this damage.
About $1,500.
Is the captain of the ' Stanley ' the man who is supposed to keep up communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland ?
Yes.
I suppose it is understood that if this item passes now it does not prevent general discussion again if it is necessary.

speechtext:

, Examination of masters and mates, $7,000.

In view of the minister refusing assent to the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Lincoln, what is going to be the policy of the department with regard to the examination of masters and mates ? It was stated last evening that the examiners were not in all cases qualified, and had not passed the necessary examination themselves ; it was also said that the examiners were paid by fees which the hon. gentleman knows is hardly the proper way to remunerate such officers.

As I stated last night, it is the intention to consolidate the laws concerning masters and mates, and also to amend the regulations as regards the examination and, the status of the examiners. I have been in the department for only eighteen months, and I cannot be expected to do everything at once. I think no one will reproach me with not attending to my duty, because I am at my office every morning at nine or half past nine, and I am trying to do the best I can. If there are many things to be remedied I do not blame my predecessors in office whether they belong to my own party or not; I suppose they did their best. There is no doubt that the demands on the department at present are very great, and I am trying to do everything which I believe to be in the interests of the department and the country generally. Of course, I am open to the charge that I belong to a party which is not in sympathy with gentlemen opposite, but my department is a department into which party politics does not enter a very great deal.
Of course not.

And party politics should not enter into my department a very great deal either, because it is a department which is charged with, developing important interests in this country, and especially the national route of the St. Lawrence. Any suggestion which comes from any part of the country or-from men of any shade of politics, will be considered by me and put into execution if I think it wise to do so, and if I have the means. I cannot say more than that.

I do not remonstrate with the hon. gentleman because he is at his office from an early hour in the morning to a late hour at night, but I think I can find fault that his splendid professions are not carried into practice.

The hon. gentleman's best is not very encouraging. I do not say that everything asked from the department should be granted, but certain things have been asked which appeal so strongly to common sense, that it puzzles one to know why the minister can waive them aside after his own light hearted fashion.
It is my natural disposition; I am born that wp.y.

I have not the least fear that the hon. gentleman will over power us by his virtue. If the hon. gentleman were less amiable and more businesslike he would serve the country better than he does. He tells us that we must wait for him to takei his office out of a state of chaos ; but he will have to afford some better reason why he did not this session consolidate the law, relating to masters and mates. I believe the minister is capable of acting vigorously, if he wants to, and I hardly think he is too short a time in his office not to have opinions of his own.
I think, without having any personal knowledge of these matters, that the hon. gentleman must be advised very much by his staff. But to receive the advice of a very good staff and to be utterly without any policy of how the department should be carried on are two very different things. I should like to know what is to be done this year-whether it is the hon. gentleman's intention to compel those making applications for certificates to conform to some healthy rules, namely, that an affidavit should be made as to their service and who they were ; that examiners should be persons who are qualified by reason of having passed the examinations themselves ; and that no inducement should be held out to any one to open the spout and turn out a batch of certificates on commission or something else. The hon. gentleman says that he hopes for a better state of things at some time ; that is all the information I have received from him.

We are aware that the hon. minister is new to the department, but he has a very able staff. At the same time, we must look after the business of the country, and I think we might allow these items to" pass without very much discussion.

I would ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to produce that letter or report from Captain Bernier.

Mr. PRE-FONTAINE. The hon. gentleman is unreasonable. Does he imagine that I am going to walk to the department and look up papers, and bring documents here of which I have had no notice whatever ?
I think it is a most unreasonable request to make of a minister and I do not intend to submit to it.

I do not think it is unreasonable at all. The hon. gentleman said it was a letter, and afterwards he called it a report ; and he said he would produce it. I do not mean that the hon. gentleman should walk to his department and get this document ; but it seems to me that he has plenty of means for getting it. This report must have been filed in his department not more than two or three days ago, so that it must be very easily obtained. Unless there is something in the report which my hon. friend does not want to show, or unless it contradicts what he said this afternoon, I cannot see any reason why he should refuse to produce it before the House. My hon. friend said this afternoon that he did not know that the papers in Quebec and Montreal had spoken about this thing.

1 never said anything of the sort. I said I did not mind the reports of the newspapers. I did not say that I did not read or take cognizance of them. I said I did not care for the reports, garbled reports mostly, and interviews made up of whole cloth. They did not concern me in any shape or form, and 1 thought Captain Bernier had taken the same view of them. The hon. gentleman has no right to put in my mouth words which I did not use.

Perhaps my understanding is at fault; but I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he had not seen what the papers said. I have in my hand ' La Presse ' of the 14tli of June, the day the ' Gauss ' arrived in Quebec. This paper is full of reports from the different members of the crew. Here is a complaint signed by almost all the crew, with an affidavit about certain matters that happened while this ship was crossing from Germany. There ds an interview with Captain Bernier, which I will read to the House :
(Translation.) He will defend himself before the competent authorities.
The following interview, by telephone, with Captain Bernier, who is in Quebec, explains the other side of the medal.
I am aware, said the captain, of the complaints made against me by my crew, but you do not expect that I will discuss them in public. I leave to those young people the responsibility for their strange course, which consists in having addressed collectively a complaint to the marine authorities, which is founded on deceptions, and in having submitted, at the same -time, that complaint to the public. Such is a discourteous proceeding that will scarcely give them any sympathy.
All that I can tell you is that the vast majority of the young men who formed my crew, had never done any navigation, and that a large number of them had never seen the sea.
It was by dint of persistent requests and the setting up of claims more or less worthless that the greater portion of my crew obtained enrolment, while I was not given the liberty to make selections.	For those
young people it was a question of a pleasure excursion, of a delightful and free trip, that would enable them, on -their return, to tell their parents, their friends and1 even those uninterested, imaginary stories of adventure
Once at work, they had- to settle down. They had been engaged to work the vessel, to labour, and that obligation entirely disillusioned them.
They say that they belong to good families; it is quite possible, I do not dispute the fact; but, then, they could have remained at home and not have taken the places of good sailors, both experienced and disciplined, whom I might have selected, and who, certainly, on their return would not have complained-seeing that life on board the ' Gauss ' would not have differed from any other voyage they might have made upon no matter what vessel.
The ' Gauss ' is not a pleasure-boat, and the voyage from Germany to Canada is not a recreation trip.
Life on board a sailing vessel, even for sailors is rough, and I can understand that these young people of good family, accustomed to the sweets of the paternal home, experienced a great disappointment on finding themselves bound to do the painful work of sailors, when they had dreamed of a tourist crossing, sheltered by a tent, or rocking themselves, cigar in mouth, in the rocking-chairs of the captain's cabin, and sipping hot or cold drinks according to taste.
The complaints of those young men are possibly sincere, but they are evidently dictated by the vexation, the disillusion, and the disappointment of not being able to parade a pompous title, all the more glorious in the fact that it would make known the ease and importance they enjoyed on board.
I am not an atom inferior to those young people, and yet, even though my employment and my title should have dispensed me therefrom, had I on board assistants of experience and broken in to the work, instead of having those accustomed to the parlour, I performed each day the ordinary work of a sailor and 'never slept more than four hours per day.
I confine my remarks on the subject to this, reserving to myself the right to give a vigorous reply to the minister, as I believe that such a discussion interests him alone, at least until such time as he passes thereon. I and that from being the accused I may before the minister, the roles will be changed, and that from being the accused I may bel come the accuser, by my complaint of a plot formed against me, as- the facts themselves establish.
Now my point is this :	My hon. friend
says that Captain Bernier has stated in a letter or report made to him that lxe never gave this interview. At first he said a letter, then he corrected that by saying a report. That may be true. It may happen



that Captain Bernier, at the time he was speaking, did not know that he was being interviewed. From personal experience 1 can say that I have conversed with a reporter sometimes not knowing that he was a reporter and I was surprised to read next day in a paper almost exactly what (I had said. I did not know that I was giving an interview, in fact I was not giving an interview, but my opinions were there all the same expressed in the newspaper. That is what may have happened to Captain 'Bernier. But in the ' Mail and Empire ' he makes these statements, he says that he was obliged to take certain men that were not fit for the job for which they were engaged, that they were not sailors, that they had never seen the sea and did not know anything about navigation ; and the consequence was that he and his chief officers were obliged to be on the bridge almost all the time, and were obliged to do the ordinary work of seamen on that ship. Now we want to know whether it is true that Captain Bernier was forced to take this crew with him as he repeats in this interview. It is published in the press, and remember it is alleged that this man Laferri&re was taken on board as a master gunner when there were no guns on the ship at all. We have this fact, at all events, stated by Captain Bernier that he was forced to take these men who were not lit for the service for which they had been engaged. Now if my hon. friend has a report or a letter, while we are on this question, it seems to me the easiest thing in the world for him to produce it. That is the request I make, . a perfectly reasonable and just request. Let him produce before this committee that letter, or dhat report. I do not ask him to read it all. There may be things in it that do not interest the public or interest this committee. But Captain Bernier has been accused by the crew before the whole community of the most inhuman treatment possible. He has been accused for instance, of having knowingly taken on board that ship provisions which were absolutely unfit for use, and the greater part of which had to be thrown overboard. He is accused in these reports, which are signed by the members of the crew of keeping these men on biscuits and butter almost the whole trip across. He is accused of ill treating his crew, and I say that it is only common justice to Captain Bernier, who is an employee of the government, who has been entrusted by the government with the command of this ship in taking it over from Germany to Canada, to let him state his case before the public so that he can vim dicate himself from these grave and serious charges. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman should, I respectfully submit, defend his officer, his employee against Mr. CASGRAIN.
these accusations. Now my hon. friend says that he is not obliged to walk over to his department and get this letter. But he has a lot of employees, and he could easily send one of them over for this letter. I say again that he ought to produce it now while the discussion is going on. If he does not produce it we shall conclude that there is something in the report which he does not want to lay before the committee, or something which contradicts the statement which he made to the House.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word upon this question. When the crew was engaged, I asked the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries if he would take on board of the * Gauss,' a person whom I was ready to recommend. The answer was : telegraph to your man to come and meet Captain Bernier at Quebec, and if he is judged competent by Captain Bernier and Captain Spain, he will be engaged.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I must say for the information of the hon. member for Montmorency, that I have myself asked Joseph Couillard, of Montmagny, as second mate on board of the ' Gauss.' The minister told me to go and see Captain Bernier, and Captain Bernier told me that he was entrusted with the selection of the crew and that if Couillard was found competent he would take him on board.
I understand that the men whom the hon. member for Temis-cuouata (Mr. Gauvreau) and the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. A. Lavergne) recommended to Captain Bernier, were refused.
The man I recommended was accepted.

Well, if Captain Bernier corroborates that statement, it justifies my hon. friend. But there is another feature to this matter to which I alluded just now. The accusation that these men brought against Captain Bernier in the public press has been published throughout the country in all the papers, and it is only fair to him that he should be cleared of itlte accusation brought against him. There is no reason' in the world why my hon. friend should not produce that report. I say that after the promise he has given to the committee it is time he should produce it. It is no justification for him to say that he cannot walk over to his department and get it. This report was handed in within the last two or three days, it must be easily obtained.

Let me say in two words that what my hon. friend from Montmorency has read from ' La Presse '

bears its own condemnation. How could Captain Bernier state what is mentioned in this interview ? It would be the most stupid thing on the part of a master of a ship to say that he left Quebec to go to Germany and bring back a ship on his own responsibility, and that, like a fool, he accepted the men that were offered to him that he was ordered to take, and now, when complaints are made, to say that he was forced to do so. I say it is so ridiculous, it is so childish, that I am" surprised that my hon. friend from Montmorency, who has had a good deal of political experience, should pay so much attention to a trifling matter of this kind. I stated before recess that Captain Bernier denied ever having given an interview to the newspapers, denied it over his own signature. Whether he did it by report, or letter, or telegram does not matter, the fact is he denied it.
The hon. gentleman would like me to take notice of what has been stated in the newspapers. As head of the department, I take no notice of these things, unless they are brought to my attention in an official way. These pretended complaints were made on the part of a few hot-headed fellows who did not know what they were about when they were engaged. These fellows have not dared, up to the present moment to lay their complaints before the department ; they have not dared lay them before Capt. Bernier. But they have gone to the newspapers. What do I care about that ? What difference does it make to the department. If these gentlemen had been sincere, if they had been serious, if they had not been playing a childish game, they would at least have taken the trouble to send me a copy of the paper in which they printed these pretended complaints. But I have nothing in the department about the matter. Under these circumstances, it seems to me childish to treat the question in this way and to try to make political capital out of it. If political capital is to be made out of it who is going to suffer ? Capt. Bernier is going to suffer, because he has declared- and he cannot deny it-that he has been left free to choose his crew. If he misjudged the men he engaged, that is his own affair. If there are serious complaints against the conduct of any officer they will be treated seriously. But there is nothing of that kind in the department. I know that it has been stated in the newspapers that unwholesome meat was served in the ship. Well, as to that we have the report of two German members of the crew, officers-the engineer and the assistant engineer-who state that on one occasion by mere accident, some preserved beef was served that was not in proper condition. To whom was it served ? It was served to the captain himself the officers and the crew. And, if these fellows, who were sea sick were particularly offended by this kind of meat, 1664
surely the captain is not to be held responsible for their feelings. The meat was bought, with other meat, from a responsible firm in Germany. It was meat that had been put up in Germany. And if it happened that some of this meat was not what it was thought to be, that is no more than might happen in any household. You may buy some meat that you think perfectly good, only to find, when it is on the table, that it is not fit to be eaten. Surely, the whole department is not to be held to blame for a thing of that kind. In a lumber camp, the same thing sometimes happens. Twenty-five barrels of beef may be provided, of which twenty-four are found to be of first-class quality, but the other one is wrong. Is that any reason why the boss of the shanty should be threatened with death, accused of attempting to poison his men and denounced ,as one who ought to be hanged ? These things are too ridiculous. It is not a serious treatment of a public question to occupy the time of the committee with such nonsensical things.
I am sorry I have excited the ire of my hon. friend (Mr. Pre-fontaine).
Not at all.

But I have attained my object to a certain extent. I have been wanting to get from my hon. friend the statement that he does not believe the accusations brought against Capt. Bernier by his crew in the press. I have sought for an hour to get from my hon. friend a vindication of the character of this man whose reputation, until now, has been of the very best. I have succeeded so far.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) will allow me-he was not in the House for a quarter of an hour or so when this question was first threshed out. What I have just stated, I stated then- that there was no official information in the department from the crew or from anybody else, and that I relied on what the captain had stated to me.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. PrSfontaine) is mistaken. I was here, and have been here during the whole of this discussion. I have not missed a single one of the eloquent words which my hon. friend has vouchsafed to utter to the committee. He started with the argument that it is perfectly ridiculous to say that Capt. Bernier should have stated anything of the kind as that he had been called upon to sail this ship with a crew that were unfit for the work for which they had been engaged. That is not the question. We have here two newspapers giving two interviews with Capt. Bernier at two different times, in which he states positively that a certain crew were foisted upon him, that he had to take them and that they were unfit for the job for which they were hired-that

they were anything but seamen. On the other hand, the minister says he has a letter, or it may be a report, or, he says now that it may be a telegram, from Capt. Bernier, denying that he gave these interviews. At first he described it as a letter over Capt. Bernier's signature. This implies a short document which could easily be produced before the House. After that, under the fire of the questions to which he was subjected, he changed his base and said that it was a report. Why ? Because a report would be a long document which it would be more difficult to bring before the House. He says now that it may be a telegram. We have a right to know what it is. We have had a suspension of the sitting of the committee for two hours and the bon. minister has had time to get this report, or letter or telegram-whichever it may be-and bring it before this committee. I state again that the reason that he does not produce it is that he is afraid that the statement contained in the letter will contradict what he has said in this committee. Is this going to be another suppression of a document ? Is this document marked ' private ' or ' confidential ' ? Is this a private document that will be brought down only if and when it helps the case of hon. gentlemen opposite ? Are we to have the suppression of a document which is asked for and which should be here when the estimates of the department are under discussion, especially after my hon. friend has said that he will produce it ? He knows very well that even if I put a notice of motion on the paper for the production of the document I should have no opportunity to move that motion this session, because yesterday was the last private members' day ? My hon. friend will not produce the document which will probably contradict his statements in this committee ; he will not produce the document which will probably be his condemnation. This is not a trifling matter, it is not a trivial matter ; it is not a matter which this committee should not discuss. I say again that the attention of the people of the province of Quebec has been called to this matter and. that ever since the ' Gauss ' arrived the press has been full of these reports and accusations. This is a matter in which the press and the public in the province of Quebec are taking a deep interest. This is not a trifling matter. When an hon. gentleman tells the House that he has a letter or a telegram, he is bound to produce it. What does the hon. gentleman mean by my experience ? Does he want me to talk about his ? I think he had better leave the question of experience alone.

We are not discussing the item of the ' Gauss ' at present. When that item comes before the House will be the proper time to produce all the documents in connection with it, and I invite the hon. gentleman then to be present. He will then see that none of the documents Mr. CASGRAIN.
which will be filed by me will contradict anything I have said. But we are not discussing that item now.
My hon. friend is wrong again. We are discussing item 191, the first sub-item of which iS maintenance and repairs' of government steamers.
That does not ap ply to the ' Gauss ' at 'all. It is not mentioned.
Is the ' Aberdeen,' or the ' Minto,' or the ' Lord Stanley ' mentioned ?
Yes ; in explaining the item I said it related to them.
The ' Gauss ' is a government steamer, and I have the right to know all about it on this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Just before the hon. gentleman came in we passed the item.
On the understanding that it could be discussed again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no objection to its being discussed, but when the point of order is raised I have to rule.

The hon. minister must know that before the item passed I rose to speak, when he consented, in reply to my hon. friend from Both well (Mr. Clancy )r that the general discussion might take place on any of the sub-items.

There must be a misunderstanding somewhere. When the item of $250,000 came before the committee, I enumerated every steamer to which it applied, and the ' Gauss ' was not mentioned' at all. When the item concerning the * Gauss ' comes up ail the documents will be produced, but I should not be asked now to produce any part of the documents. There is an investigation to be made by Capta in-Spain, and Captain Spain's report will be-submitted. The,proper time to submit every document will be when the item is submitted, and that can only be in the supplementary estimates.

I arise more particularly to vindicate our rights as an opposition. On this item of repairs to government steamers I claim that we have the right to discuss the ' Gauss ' or any other steamer owned by the government. Last year on this same item we discussed the maintenance and repairs and sale of government steamers, which had gone out of the possession of the government. This may not be the most opportune time to discuss matters connected with the ' Gauss,' but we have the right to do It.

Well, I do not think it is right to ask me to produce a part of the documents and bring down an incomplete return on an Item that does not affect this particular steamer, the ' Gauss," at all.
Jilts E 21. 1904

We are here discussing the repairs to government steamers, anti are not to be silenced. There is a very easy way of settling this matter, and that is by moving that the committee rise. The hon. gentleman is in a corner and is. trying to get out of it. I have had him in a corner before in other eases. He is simply raising the point of order so as to prevent discussion. He is bound to produce this letter and refuses to do so, probably either because it contradicts his statement or does not exist. I have made the charge and the country can judge between us.
Supposing there was no expenditure on the ' Stanley,' have we not the right to discuss anything relating to that vessel on this item 1

speakeroldname: Mr. P REF O NT AIN E.
speechtext: I have not said that you have not.
Does the hon. gentleman say that Captain Bernier was given a free hand in selecting his crew ?
Yes.	[DOT]

At Owen Sound, where there are two government vessels, it was the custom up to 1896 to leave the selection of the crew to the captains. In 1896 the president of the Liberal Association practically dictated to the captains of these vessels the men they should employ, and what was the result ? Why, take the crew of the ' Petrel,' and if it landed at any town in Canada it was a pleasure to see that crew go ashore. There was uniformity in size and there was discipline.
Hear, hear.

I mean before 1896. To-day you have no unifomity in size, and if it was ever intended for a small navy it has deteriorated under the present system. The captains do not select the crews, but are dictated to, not by the minister or by any official of the department, but by the president of the Liberal Association in that riding.

I wish to refer again to the sale of the steamer ' Bayfield,' which was discussed last year. On page P-164 of the Auditor General's Report will be found some very severe strictures by the Auditor General upon this transaction, by which this boat was sold for half her value to a friend, not a personal friend of the minister, but to a firm who are strong political friends and allies of hon. gentlemen opposite. The letter to which I refer is as follows :
Audit Office, Ottawa, June 10, 1903.
Sir,-I have received your letter of the 6th instant, inclosing a report of Wffl. J. Stewart of your department, dated February 17, 1903, in which he values the steamer ' Bayfield ' at $7,000. With that letter is inclosed also the
offer of $3,250 hy John Harrison & Sons Co. for the vessel, dated March 12, and on this letter is a note signed by Wm. J. Stewart recommending the acceptance of the offer. No explanation is furnished why Mr. Stewart valued the vessel at $t,000 on February 17 and recommended her sale in March for $3,250.
Was the vessel valued by any other officer or builder-the captain in charge, for instance ?
Was there any reason to fear that the country might have suffered by calling for tenders in this case.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
J. L. McDOUGALL, A.G. The Deputy Minister, Marine and Fisheries.
In the last few lines of this letter I think there is 'a certain amount of sarcasm-
Was there any reason to fear that the country might have suffered hy calling for tenders in this case ?
Here is an official of the department in February stating that the vessel in his opinion is worth $7,000 and within a month, in the fulness of his heart and his great liberality, he hands her over to party friends for $3,250. No excuse as to the uuseaworthiness of the vessel will serve, because her new owners have employed her on the Georgian bay waters in all kinds of weather towing logs, not only risking the vessel, but valuable rafts of logs behind her. Thus the vessel was in a seaworthy condition when She was sold, and the minister, without any authority or any right from parliament, or even from his colleagues in the cabinet, because there was no Order in Council, turned around and makes a present of the vessel to party friends for half its value.

Last year I gave all explanations in connection with this, and I have nothing to add to what I then stated, which can be read in ' Hansard.' I stand by the bargain of last year, which I think was the best that could be made under the circumstances. If the hon. gentleman wants to use it as campaign literature, as he said last year he did, he is welcome to it. I have read the Conservative papers since then, but I do not see that it was contained in any of the pamphlets since published. In order to put the thing as clearly as possible before the House, I shall read a letter which I have here from John Harrison & Sons Company, Limited, the present owners of the vessel, which bears out what I said last year.
