I said that the disposal of the boat at $3,250 was a good sale, because the boat was a charge to the department and could not be used satisfactorily for the work to J>e done ; the officers would not risk their lives on her on Georgian bay waters, and she had to be sold. We took offers, and the offer of John Harrison & Sons Company, Limited, was considered the best, and a reasonable offer.

Stewart, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, an oid employee of the department, appointed under the old government before 1896, a man not likely to be suspected of any leanings towards our party, took upon himself to make the recommendation. I myself knew nothing of the boat, and the other officers of the department here did not know anything of her value or of the opportunity of selling her. We relied entirely on the recommendation of Commander Stewart and on the opinion of other officers who have technical knowledge. The letter of Messrs. Harrison & Sons Company, Limited, is as follows :
Owen Sound, Ont., Canada,
March 25th, 1904.

Stewart,
Department of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa.
Dear sir,-With reference to the old steamer ' Bayfield,' now the * Harrison,' which we purchased from the department about a year ago, owing to some unfair remarks made by some of the members last session, we feel it our duty to advise your department that as we expected at the time we purchased this boat, we now have to put in a new engine. Though the old engine is still as good as when we bought the boat, on account of it being weak at the .main bearing and a high pressure engine that would consume a larger quantity of coal than could be paid for out of her earnings, we are unable to sell the old engine for more than scrap iron price and have already disposed of it for this purpose. We have not yet received the weights, but expect to realize about $190 out of the engine.
We have to put in a new' engine, shaft and propellor this winter, as well as other necessary repairs and when we get through we will have a boat that is in her .forty-second year.
However, we happen to have a lot of timber to move on the Georgian bay and hope to use her to advantage in our own work.
Thinking it possible there might be something further said regarding this during the present session, we wish you would be good enough to give the department these particulars.
Thanking you for your favour.
We remain, &c.,
'Sgd.) JOHN HARRISON & SONS Co., LTD.
These are the facts in a nut shell. I knew nothing of the boat myself, I acted entirely on the opinion of my officers especially that of Mr. Stewart who had used the boat on the Georgian bay for surveys, and who considered her unsafe. Mr. Stewart declared that neither his assistants nor himself would risk their lives in it, and that is borne out by the letter of the purchaser who said that they could not use the boat without renewing the engine, because she would consume more coal than she could earn.
The minister should have read to the House the letter written by the department asking the Harrison people to write that letter.
There is no such letter in the department. I did not know of the existence of the letter until just now and I am informed that it was addressed to Mr. Stewart voluntarily.
It seems odd that Mr. Harrison should go to the trouble of writing this letter. The defence of the minister now is that he acted exclusively on the opinion of Mr. Stewart.
Not exclusively. I consulted Mr. McElhinney our technical nautical adviser and he concurred in the opinion of Mr. Stewart.

There is nothing in Mr. Stewart's letter saying that the boat was unsafe. He writes : To-day I think she is worth $7,000. Yet in the face of that report the minister deliberately makes her a present to one of his party friends for. $3,250. I admit that they put a new engine in her, but this only goes to prove that the hull was sound. The minister has also a report from the captain that a party in Owen Sound was willing to give $5,000 for the boat.
Where is that offer ?

Mr. Stewart's letter of the 9th of February says :
I telegraphed Captain McGregor and Mr. Nisbit, the engineer, for valuations. The former answered $7,000, that is as to her value. I could get $5,000 cash for her in Goderich.
That	offer	was on	record in	the department,	'and	yet the	minister	spurns the$5,000	and	sells her	to party	friends for$3,250.	Last	year the	excuse of the minister
was that the cost of advertising would amount to a couple of thousand dollars, but we had not those letters before us to show that he could get $5,000 for her in the town of Goderich.
Does the hon. gentleman know that when this offer was accepted the man backed out of it ?
Will the minister produce the statement from the Harrisons that they backed out of that bargain for $5,000 ?
They never made an offer of $5,000.
Certainly they did not, because they had the minister's assurance that he was going to make a present of it for $3,250.
That is pure fabrication ; that is invention.
It is fabrication on the part of the minister who said that the Har-' risons endeavoured to get out of that Bargain.
I never said anything of the kind. I said with regard to the pretended offer of $5,000, that the parties did not come up to the scratch.
Who made the offer of $5,000 ?
I don't know.
There was the report of Captain Stewart that a man in Goderich would pay $5,000 cash for her.
Instructions were given to Captain McGregor to close the bargain for $5,000, and the result was that the man did not come up with the money.

It is curious that all the documents the minister can get on record are those which implicate him, and that he did not send Any of these exculpating documents to the Auditor General when that official wrote to him asking if he were afraid that at an open sale the boat would bring a higher price. The fact is that the minister in the fulness of his good nature- and I am willing to attribute to the minister a large fund of that quality when he is dealihg with the public property and when at the same time he is endeavouring to ingratiate himself with his supporters; particularly in the province of Ontario-in the fulness of his good nature, notwithstanding that his officers valued the boat at $7,000, he sells her to the Harrison people, who are very important Liberals in the town of Owen Sound, for $3,250. I admire the good nature of the Minister of Marine, but it is unfortunate that he practices it at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. I have another example of that in my own riding. A few weeks ago in the fulness of his heart, he made a party friend a present of $4,000 or $5,000 worth of timber for $100. The Minister of Marine wants to make a reputation for himself as a good fellow, at the public expense and particularly with his supporters in Ontario, and here he gives a large tract of valuable timber in the riding of Hast Simcoe for a paltry $100, which if it had been put on the open market would have sold at from $3,000 to $5,000. The minister must know that while he may defy public opinion by giving away that which is not his without open competition, so far as I am concerned I will discuss these matters.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to a promise which he made to me on Friday last. We were discussing the placing of buoys in the Napanee river, and I asked him for the correspondence that had taken place between Mr. Mowers and those who represent him and the department. He promised to send me the information last Saturday by mail. I do not know whether he mailed it or not, but I know that it has not reached me.

I do not remember that the hon. gentleman asked for the correspondence. I remember that the question was brought up, and I said I would give the information, and I am ready with the information at the present moment. In 1903 the department made a contract with Mr. Blakely Mowers, of Napanee, to perform the buoy service on the Napanee river at $60 per annum. The contract was made for one year instead of three, because the department expected to take up this buoy service with the steamer ' Scout ' some time during 1904. The contract of Mr. Mowers was dated 1st June, 1903, to terminate one year from the date of it. Mr. Mowers was paid $60 for the work of 1903. It was expected that he would place the buoys in the spring of 1904, and he was instructed to do so on the 10th May last, and informed that his contract did not terminate until 1st June, 1904. A letter was received from Mr. R. A. Leonard on the 7th May last, on behalf of Mr. Mowers and another from Mr. W. S. Herrington. Copies of the answers to these letters are attached. They show that Mr. Mowers was instructed to place the buoys, and also informed that the department would pay for placing them this spring in addition to what had been paid before. It has been found that the ' Scout ' could not attend to the. buoy service this year, but it was expected that Mr. Mowers would place the buoys in accordance with the terms of his contract and furnish his account for payment. On the 2Gth of May, Mr. Herrington stated that if the department would make clear that Mr. Mowers was to be paid for placing the buoys this spring, he would go on with the work. He was a second time assured, through Mr. Herrington who wrote his letters, that he would be paid for putting out the buoys. The department has no harbour master or other officer at Napanee to superintend the work. Tenders have been invited for placing the buoys for the next three years.
There is no objection to giving the bon. gentleman a copy of all the correspondence.
When shall I get it ?
As soon as it can be copied.
The hon. minister promised me before dinner a list of the grocers in Quebec who asked leave to tender for supplies.	,
The hon. gentleman will get it within the next twenty-four hours.
Now is the time to have it.
The hon. gentleman does not suppose that I am going to send for all the books of the department and have them laid on the table of the House.

Not at all. The hon. minister does not need to go through all the books of the department to get the names of these grocers. There are not more than three or four of them. I never before saw a minister refuse such information when his estimates were up.
The hon. gentleman has no right to say that I refused information when I tell him that it will be before the House in the next twenty-four hours.
What the hon. gentleman says amounts to a refusal, because he knows that within twenty-four hours we shall be probably off this item.
Whether we are off this item or not, the list will be on the table of the House to-morrow.,

But I have some remarks to make, and I cannot make them until I have the names. Now is the time to have them. We cannot get information from this department, because the fact is that the hon. gentleman does not know anything about his department. We have got no information about any of the items brought before the committee, although we have tried to get it. We have used a corkscrew to get the information from the hon. gentleman, but the corkscrew does not work.

I am beginning to think that the reputation of the minister for good nature is so well known that people take advantage of it. I think that was the case with the Harrison firm of Owen Sound. I thought, after the disclosures that had been made, that the minister would have come here in a penitent frame of mind, and would have assured the House if any sales of timber or anything else were to be made la future, the wholesome rule of open tender would be followed. But the minister is hard-hearted. He is asking this com-Mr. WILSON.
mittee to vote him large sums of money as a minister of the Crown. It is not only in reference to the moneys entrusted to him, but also in reference to any part of the public domain in his charge tiiat we have a perfect right to discuss his actions ; and in that connection I propose to discuss the question of giving away a large quantity of very valuable timber on a lighthouse reserve on the Georgian bay. Among other islands on which lighthouses are situated is the Hope island, one of the group called the Christian Islands. This island has for a long time been regarded as a very rich timber reserve. Of course, it was under the Department of Indian Affairs, and a few years ago, on representations made by the Marine Department, the Indian Department gave a hundred acres of timber land on that island to the Marine Department. It was never expected that this was going to be exploited by party friends, but it was given with a view of affording eordwood for the lighthouse-keeper on that island. To the surprise of the Indians, who had given it up for nothing, and a number of Liberals in that part of the country who for years have cast longing eyes on that reserve, last winter a party friend made application to the hon. minister through a member of this House, and without any competition that one hundred acres of valuable timber was handed over to him for a pittance of $100. I am going to read the correspondence in connection with this matter.
First, let me state that it was no vile Tory who got this property. It will be fair to assume that it was a close personal ally of hon. gentlemen opposite, and that close'personal ally was not my opponent in the last campaign and my prospective opponent in the next, but his son and business partner. Here was the timber on this 100 acres of land-certain parts of it referred to in the correspondence-sold without competition to the partners of the ex-Liberal candidate in that riding for the sum of $100. Had that timber been sold by public auction it would have brought considerably over $3,000 The correspondence started in 1903, and.the following letter was written on the 19th of August :
House of Commons,
Ottawa, August 19th, 1903.
Dear Mr. Prefontaine,-A constituent of mine is desirous of purchasing the cedar and basswood timber on the lot owned by your department on Hope Island in Georgian hay. Your department bought the tract to supply fuel for lighthouse and require only hardwood.
Col. Anderson, whom I saw to-day, informs me that it is the practice to sell the soft wood and that he recommends the sale provided I arrange price with you.
My correspondent tells me that cedar and basswood is sprinkling only and much of it blown down. It rots quickly thus. He offers $100 for the cedar and basswood, asking that he

523&
be allowed two or three years to remove 'it, at the same time not to damage your hardwood.
Duck island, Col. Anderson tel IS me, was so disposed of. My own acquaintance with the Hope island convinces me that the price is fair, as in the 100 acres. When the beech and maple is so thick there cannot be a great deal of cedar or basswood and hemlock.
Perhaps you would be good enough to intimate to me what further assurance, if any, is required, that I may write my friend, and to note for the meantime his formal application.
Very sincerely yours,

In the first place, my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Grant) makes the statement that Mr. Chew is a .constituent of his, but as a matter of fact he is not. He is a resident of East Simcoe and not of North Ontario. I admit that the hon. minister might have obtained the idea from that letter of handing over the property for the sum of $100, because the hon. member for North Ontario assures him that he knows Hope island and that the price is a fan-one. This island is some thirty miles from Midland. I have been on it once, and I know it is heavily wooded. I do not know how many times the hon. gentleman was over that island or what knowledge he has of the value of timber, but even if, in the face of his personal assurance, the minister might have been somewhat misled, it was the duty of the minister to have put that timber up at public auction. I am going to give all the facts, because I grant that the minister did do something in the premises which perhaps may buttress the position he took afterwards. A letter was written by the department to the lighthouse keeper asking him to report on the value of the timber. Perhaps I had better read that letter :
Ottawa, 25th August, 1903.
Sir,-Hr. Grant, M.P., writes the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that a constituent of his is desirous of purchasing the cedar and basswood timber on the lot owned by this department on Hope island, the tract of land upon which the timber grows having been bought by the department to supply fuel for the lighthouse, but that hardwood is only required for that purpose. Mr. Grant further states that the practice has been to sell the soft wood, much of which is blown down as it rots quickly, and the purchaser is allowed two or three years to remove it, precautions being taken that he does not damage the hardwood.	<
I have to request you to report to the department as to the quantity of basswood and cedar you suppose Is on the land In question, and to state what you consider would be a fair price therefor.
X want to call attention particularly to this fact, that when the deputy minister writes to the lighthouse keeper he only asks a report on the basswood and cedar, and makes no mention of any other kind of timber. This lighthouse keeper has his lighthouse some twenty miles away from the
post office, and it has been suggested to me that intimation was given certain parties that the letter would be waiting the lighthouse keeper at the post office. Be that as it may, the letter did reach the lighthouse keeper, and I want the House to listen carefully to his report:
I think it is a wise idea to sell all the soft wood, because there is a good deal of it going to waste every year.
As to 'the quantity of basswood and cedar in feet, there is between fifty and sixty thousand feet to the best I can judge.
Is it not very likely that the interested parties took the letter out to the lighthouse keeper and suggested to him his report, because, although he was only asked to report on the cedar and basswood, he goes on to report on the hemlock and elm 7 The fact is that Mr. Chew wanted to get, not only the cedar and the basswood, but the hem-iock and elm, and persuaded the lighthouse keeper to give a favourable report. I tell the hon. minister now what he ought to know, because an official of his department lias been out there of late. In order to get a favourable report from the lighthouse keeper, they gave him a contract for taking off the timber. Here you have this man acting in a double capacity. You find him acting as agent for the department and at the same time as contractor for the party applying to the department. Is the hon. minister aware that his lighthouse keeper was busy some months with three or four men taking off part of the timber 7
I knew nothing about it.
Does the hon. gentleman know now 7
I do not.

The hon. gentleman's official must have known about it, because he was out there a few weeks ago. Here is the whole plan laid bare. First they endeavoured to get in touch with the lighthouse keeper so as to secure a favourable report. How did they do that 7 They pointed out to him that he could put in his days taking off the timber, and that would not interfere with his attending to the lights at night. After the deal was carried out, the $100 were handed over to the department by the hon. member for North Ontario. Mr. Chew was then given the timber. Forthwith Mr. Chew put in a large complement of men. I am informed that there were some fifteen men there two and a half months, with three teams of horses, getting out timber during the past winter from that island.
I am informed that there were some fifteen men and three teams there for two months and a half. And I have information_and information that I believe to be
correct-tiiat not less than 150.000 feet of

lumber were taken off the island. It is all right for the hon. gentleman to try to shelter himself behind the statement that this was fallen timber. But any one who knows anything of the nature of basswood knows that basswood that had fallen would be utterly useless, because it is a kind of timber that rots quickly. And any one who knows anything of the value of timber, knows that basswood in the form of boards is worth at least $30 a thousand feet. It is a desirable class of wood and hard to get. Well, the minister, on the report of the hon. member for North Ontario who pledges his word that, from his acquainj tauce with the island the timber is worth $100 and of the lighthouse keeper who says that itf is worth $200 the hon. gentleman passes it over to the party's nominee in the riding for $100. I called his attention to it and I moved for the correspondence, and I am informed that he allowed the party to take the timber that, despite what the hon. gentleman has said, I am informed is worth over $1,000. Then, where is the minister with respect to the balance ? These parties are allowed to take off the balance. And the Indians on the reserve are protesting most vigorously against this timber being handed over to the hon. minister's party friends. In his zeal to please his party friends he has done in this case what he did in the case of the 1 Bayfield.' The hon. gentleman seems to take the position that, no matter what it costs the country, the party's friends must be provided for in order that the minister may get the reputation of being a good fellow, even at the public expense. The hon. gentleman must learn-at least-we must endeavour to teach him-that the public domain and vessels owned by the Dominion are not his personal property ; and, if they are to be sold, they must be sold in the honest, wholesome manner of public competition, so that the people may get a fair return for what they sell.
1 I had occasion to visit home a couplq of weeks ago. Mr. Chew came to me and said :	What are you doing about that
timber ? Why don't you let me take it away ? I said:	I have nothing to do
with it ; I am only making a protest against the department giving away the public property without competition. It is not proper and it is not fair. Instead of giving you this timber for $100, it should have been offered by public competition and let everybody have a chance at it. In the course of conversation Mr. Chew told me some fiu'ther circumstances of the case. And when I said he was getting a big thing in having this timber sold to him for $100, he said he had to pav $50 more. I said: Why in the name of all that iys good, had you to pay $50 more ? He answered :	I had to enter into communi-

cation with the brother of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant) and had to pay him $50 for his services. So, what do we find the proposition to come to ? A gentleman outside makes a representation to a member of the House, and the member of the House makes a personal representation to the minister. I do not know whether my hon. friend from North Ontario will say that he has been on the island and has a knowledge of the value of the timber, or that what he represented in the matter was based on his acquaintance with the locality and knowledge of the value of timber, buc there is the statement of Mr. Chew, made before half a dozen people and quite openly, that he had to pay $50 to a gentleman on the outside to get the timber. Mr. Chew naturally asks why, if the department want to sell the timber to him for $100 he should not have it. If Mr. Chew or anybody else can get $3,000 or $4,000 worth of property for $100, that is not his fault. The fault lies with the department in allowing it to be done. This kind of thing will incite others to make raids on the treasury. True, it is not a big raid. It does not bear the same proportions as the Grand Trunk Pacific or the purchase of the Canada Eastern Railway. But it seems to be the policy of this government, in small matters as in great, and in every department, to have men on the outside who can use influence to bring about such results as we see here. The brother of the hon. member for North Ontario gets $50 out of the transaction, Mr. Chew gets $3,000 or $4,000 worth of timber, and the long-suffering country gets $100. I think it is only fair to this committee and to the country that some explanation of the matter should be given by the hon. gentleman who presides over the department.
The contract which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) holds in his hand speaks for itself.
Oh, oh.	.

I do not see anything to laugh at. I say the contract speaks for itself. The timber on the island was sold for $100 on the representation that it was worth $100. Some people say it was worth more. Well, when it is cut down and transported and sawn into boards I suppose it is worth more. But I suppose also that the man who does all this work expects to get something for it.

If the hon. minister will allow me, there is one matter that I forgot. I find-and I am confident that the minister will not deny it-that instead of restricting himself to the cutting of cedar and basswood, this gentleman has trespassed and cut other timber as well.

Well, is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) prepared to say that this party is relieved from paying for what he has cut ? If he says that, on what authority does he say it ? How can the department, here in Ottawa having made a bargain, infallibly prevent people at a distance from going beyond the terms of that bargain ? The contract as I said, speaks for itself. The man had a right to take a certain quantity of timber which was recommended to be sold as being of scarcely any value, the sale being to the advantage of the department. If the timber is said to be worth a good deal more, surely some proof of that should be offered. But it is said that other timber was cut by Mr. Chew. It was because information of that fact came to the department that an official was sent up to investigate. He found that more timber had been cut than was contracted for, and so a stumpage of $2 a thousand feet was charged Mr. Chew before he could take away the timber that was not included in his contract. Where, then, is the blame to the department ? It is said that $50 was paid to some gentleman outside. I do not know on what ground that allegation was made. But, in any case, in what way can it affect the department when the department have taken all the necessary precautions to secure the public interest ? If Mr. Chew has chosen to cut more timber than he had a right to cut under his contract, he will be called upon to pay for it-that is all.

On the 10th of May last I wrote to the minister a letter in the course of which I asked whether any officer of his department had been cutting under contract for Mr. Chew, and was still doing so. I do not know whether any of the logs have been removed or not. But, on the 10th of May he had an intimation that either the lighthouse keeper or some one else in his department-and it could hardly be any one else-had been doing the cutting for Mr. Chew. He had then an opportunity to find out whether the department had been overreached or not. He had had an opportunity to find out since. I do not know what this report is, but I am going to ask the minister if he has an official report of the quantity of timber that was cut and lying on the shore, and what was the quantity ?
The minister admits a stumpage of 140,000 feet, in addition to basswood and cedar cut under contract.

How could it be
proven ? It is a fact that has come to my knowledge only lately. But I am investigating the whole matter, and if the lightkeeper has been at fault he will suffer for it. I could not look after things of that kind before they are all over. There is a lightkeeper on Wallace island, who is defended by hon. members opposite, and who pretends that he owns Wallace island and he has sold $300 worth of property off the island to Mr. Morris, of Ottawa, and has collected the money. And now, because we are installing an automatic light at that place, he complains of all sorts of things, says that he is being despoiled, and has been deprived of what belongs to him, whereas the property belongs really to the government. These things will happen, and if this lightkeeper is at fault he will be dealt with accordingly. But until the government loses a cent, it is no use making such an outcry about it. We have acted in good faith, and on the information furnished to the department.

I know nothing about the Morris case. But I do know this, that here the minister had a valuable lot of timber on that island for the sale of which he admits to-day he has made a contract, and made it without competition, which he should not have done, and that after the party goes in there and cuts without leave or license from the department 140,000 feet of timber the minister instead as he should have done, saying to these parties: You have broken faith with the department and I will not permit you to have anything to do with this timber,-tarns round and gives it to him at a stumpage of $2 a thousand. I want to tell the minister that hemlock timber today is worth $14 to $16 a thousand.
Where does the hon. gentleman get that information ? Does he get it from any lumberman in the country ?
I do not know what came out of that bubble ; I never saw much come out of that bubble.
If the hon. gentleman gets the information that hemlock is worth $15 a thousand he gets it from some one who knows nothing about the business.
Of soft wood, about 1,500 sticks.
And in thousand feet, how much ?
In thousand feet of lumber which Mr. Chew is being charged for and for which he has consented to pay, there is 140,000 feet, for which he pays a stumpage of $2 per thousand.

I have paid more than than for it myself last year. Now here is the opinion of the minister. He had no right at all to act on this assurance of the member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant) as to the value of the timber. He knew that the member for North Ontario was not a practical lumberman. I do not know whether the minister had any conversation or not with that hon. gentleman, and whether the latter told him how many times he had been

on that island in order to ascertain the value of the timber. But I do know that when this timber was there for sale the minister should have made himself acquainted with its value, and when he found that he had been overreached by these parties, when he had fair notice that grave suspicion existed, that his own lighthouse keeper had not made a proper report on the value, he should at once have escheated ojr taken over the whole timber and sold it to the highest bidder, instead of handling it over to these people at $2 a thousand. In that part of the country where the deal is known the minister's conduct is not thought highly of.

I cannot allow the remarks of the hon. member for Bast Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) regarding myself to pass unchallenged. My whole connection with this matter is set forth in the correspondence brought down on motion of the hon. gentleman. It shows conclusively that I acted in the matter simply out of courtesy to the gentleman who is a constituent of the hon. member for Bast Simcoe. It is quite true, as has been pointed out, that in the first part of my letter I made a lapsus pennae when I used the ordinary term, which is customary in such a letter, in saying that he was a constituent of mine, and the hon! gentleman has seen fit to take exception to that remark. As a matter of fact. Mr. Chew is not a constituent of mine, but he has the distinguished honour of being a constituent of the hon. member for East Simcoe. He sent me an application in regard to Hope island, asking to purchase the soft wood on that island which is the property of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I considered myself in duty bound to file that application with the department, as I shall always consider myself in duty bound, while 1 am a member of this House, to file the application of any gentleman, Reform or Conservative, in my part of the country, who wishes to do business with the department.
I considered it an act of courtesy due to the applicant. Now the hon. member for East Simcoe has seen fit to go further in reference to my connection with this matter than my letter goes, and he says that I urged the sale of this timber upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. My letter will speak for itself on that subject. It is a portion of the return brought down, and a reference to that letter will show that I said that so far as my opinion went I thought $100 was a fair price for the soft wood, seeing that it was blown down.
Had you gone over this land to see the timber before you made that report ?

I wish to draw attention to the fact that the hon. member for Bast Simcoe has seen fit entirely to exclude from his speech the letter which I wrote on the 25th of August, in which I said that I believed, from the information given me, that the Mr. BENNETT.
offer was a fair one, and furthermore I said : ' Of course, I cannot speak from personal knowledge, but I have reason to believe that the estimate is a fair one.' That was my statement, and by that statement I will stand. A number of persons told me, whose veracity I had no reason then to doubt, and that I have no reason now to doubt, that timber of the description mentioned was worth that sum of money, or thereabouts. The papers containing my application to the department show my whole and sole connection with the matter, as will be seen by the letters filed and brought down in the return. The hon. gentleman makes a reference to supposed conversations which he thinks must have taken place between the minister- and myself. So far as my memory serves me, I think I am within the mark in saying that there was no conversation between the minister and myself regarding the matter. My connection with is is wholly disclosed in the correspondence, showing that I acted simply out of courtesy in passing on to the department the application of Mr. Chew. More than that, the hon. gentleman makes a comment upon the purchase price, if I did not mistake his remarks.
That is so endorsed on the original papers. There is a memorandum endorsed which says : ' Memo, $100 was paid in by Mr. Grant, M.P.'

My recollection of the matter is that the letter received by me from Mr. Chew inclosed the sum of money mentioned in the letter, $100 which I forwarded on to the department. I simply did on that occasion as any other hon. gentleman in this House would do. I did not keep the money, as we have heard of some other hon. gentlemen doing on a previous occasion in this House. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not know what the hon. gentleman's reference or insituation means.
I have only this to say and to say it most emphatically, that so far as this transaction is concerned, I acted simply as a matter of courtesy to a gentleman who lives in the same county as myself. I undertook nothing as to values, except to say that as far as I knew the island, and as far as I had been informed in reference to the timber on it, the price seemed to be a fair one. Now, as to the question of the hon. member for Addington (Mr. Avery) I have not traversed this island, I have passed it in the Georgian bay and have seen it. and from my observation and from the fact that it was bought for lighthouse supply purposes, for which hardwood only is required, I am convinced that it is not-apt to be very heavily timbered with soft w'ood, particularly as there is only 100 acres in all involved. The hon. gentleman has not only not been fair, but has not disclosed all that the return brought down will disclose. As a matter of fact the lighthouse keeper to whom the question of values

was referred, reports to 1,he department that there are four kinds of soft wood on the island. He says :
I consider that the cedar, the basswood, the hemlock and the elm are worth about $200.
Now the department concluded to sell to Hr. Chew not all these four kinds of timber but simply all the cedar and basswood, .iust half the timber, and it requires little mathematical skill to prove that if the four lands of timber are not worth more than $200 [DOT]the cedar and the basswood are not worth a very large amount of money. I do not know whether or not some hemlock or wood other than that specified in the agreement has been cut by Mr. Chew. With that I am not concerned, for I am sure that if that has been done the minister will see that it is paid for at a fair market price.
I desire to call attention to the fact that the conditions under which Manley Chew bought the timber from the Marine Department are extremely onerous. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) quoted from the agreement but did not quote the onerous conditions which must necessarily result in a considerable reduction in the value of the timber bought under these conditions, ft is an agreement dated September 4, 1903, whereby Manley Chew agrees to purchase from the department, &c., &c.
The timber cut under this agreement shall consist oi cedar and basswood only.
Which endorses my statement of a moment ago that the hemlock was not included in the agreement for sale, but was included in the estimate of the value made by Mr. Vallee. As I understand the purpose oif the Marine Department in acquiring this and other lighthouse plots is to have hardwood available for lighthouses "and lighthouse keepers. It is part of the policy of the department to part with the soft wood which is not necessary and which is a source of danger as it is apt to fall down and ignite. In most cases of course the lighthouses are remote from any habitation and it is very necessary that the greatest possible precaution be taken against fire. For that reason the department is frequently anxious to get rid of soft wood. More than that, as the agreement sets forth, they .require the person taking the soft wood to carefully underbrush the places where he cuts the wood, and where roads are made, and to cord the wood taken from the roadways for the lighthouse keeper. I leave it to any practical lumberman if the appending of such onerous conditions as those in the contract will not considerably reduce the value of the timber taken under these circumstances. More than that the hon. gentleman has not stated that this timber is situated on an island which is, if I am not mistaken, some thirty or forty miles from the nearest available sawmili. I have been informed by Mr. Chew that as a matter of fact, owing to the
expense involved in establishing a camp on the island and getting out the timber, he has not made a copper out of this transaction. I do not know how much timber Mr. Chew has taken from the 100 acres, and of course if he has taken timber not covered by the agreement he should pay the department and the country for it, and I have no doubt he will do so. That of course is a matter for the Minister of Marine. The question as to how much standing timber there is even on as small an area as 100 acres is always more or less open to speculation. I do not know how much Mr. Chew has taken out and it is not a matter of particular moment to me. I know however the estimate that the Department of Marine, acting on the advice of their officer living on the spot, placed upon it. The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has seen fit to insinuate that the lighthouse keeper who made this report has been tampered with in some way.
I understood him to say that the report should not be relied upon owing to the fact that the lighthouse keeper has been employed by Mr. Chew at a daily wage for cutting down some of this timber.
I do not know particularly what the character of the lighthouse keeper is ; but I understand that he has been there for some years and, so far as my information goes, he is not the sort of man who would be turned aside from doing his duty in the public service by the offer of a day's pay for a day's work. It is not creditable to the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) to make such insinuations in this House against a man in humble circumstances, a man who lives on a remote island, and who is in no way capable of defending himself against such attacks. I am here to say that so far as I know Charles Vallee is an honest man, and a man who could not be bribed. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has seen fit to refer to a brother of mine, who is a practising solicitor in the town of Midland. I would not expect the hon. member for East Simcoe to rise to speak on any matter in this House without making some personal and, perhaps, offensive allusion to one of ins fellow-members, no matter how remote the subject he is discussing may be from such a personal reference. The hon. gentleman has seen fit to say that when the sale of the timber on Hope island went through, as a coincidence, or as a complement, or, he almost said, as a condition of its going through, the sum of $50 was paid to the brother of the member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant). I do not know whether that money was paid to my brother or not; I do not know whether or not he got that money for his services, but I know he is a prac tising solicitor in the town of Midland, and if he is like some of the other solicitors practising in that town, I expect he wii! collect his fees. It is not so very long since we had it disclosed in this House that the

hon. member for East Simcoe, in a transaction which occurred between him and this same Mr. Chew, or a relative of his, in relation to a dock site in Midland involving $400, tolled Mr. Chew to the extent of $30 or $40 for solicitor's fees. The record will show that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett), or his firm, benefited to that extent. As I understand it, my 'brother has been acting of late as Mr. Chew's solicitor. I do not know that the hon. member for Eas! Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) quarrels with Mr. Frederick Grant because he is acting as solicitor for Mr. Chew, but I suppose Mr. Chew is at liberty to make any choice he wishes. If Mr. Chew employs the firm or Storey & Grant to send an application down here, to transact the necessary correspondence, to see to the conditions of the agreement, and to do all that is necessary for the closing up of this transaction with the Marine Department, I have nothing to do with that. Neither have I to do with the further fact that Mr. Chew paid that law firm their fees. Mr. Chew is free, I suppose, to deal with the firm of Storey & Grant in Midland, with which I have no connection in the world, and it may be that he was charged a fee for the legal business in connection with this transaction. The hon gentleman (Mr. Bennett) did not find the generosity in his nature to state fully to the House the fact, which he knew very well, that Mr. Frederick Grant was rt practising solicitor in Midland. The hon. gentleman knew very well that if Mr. Frederick Grant got $40 or $50, he got that as a fee for acting as a solicitor in the case. The hon. member tells us that Mr. George Chew himself told him that he paid the fee. But still the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) would leave the House under the impression that Mr. Frederick Grant was rewarded in some degree for procuring for Mr. Chew the purchase of this timber. As a matter of fact,
1 do not suppose that the Minister of Marine is at all acquainted with the firm of Storey & Grant practising in the town of Midland. At all events, they had a perfect right to collect their professional fees. We have the word of the hon. member (Mr. Bennett), which I am prepared to take, that Mr. Chew told him he paid a firm of lawyers in Midland $50 for attending to the business in connection with this matter. Weil, that law firm has as much right to charge for their services as the hon. member's firm has to be paid for their services in connection with the transaction which was ventilated on the floor of this House within the last few weeks. But perhaps this whole matter, as between the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) and Mr. Chew, is explicable by the fact that Mr. Chew is the prospective Liberal candidate in East Simcoe. No doubt the hon. member for East Simcoe takes this chance in the House, as he takes very many other chances, to discount in advance the gentleman who, it is

rumoured, will be his opponent in the next election. As a matter of fact, I understand that Mr. George Chew has personally absolutely no interest in this matter, but that Mr. Manley Chew, who is a relative of Mr. George Chew, the Liberal candidate in East Simcoe, is the person concerned. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) will not succeed in his tactics to discount Mr. Chew before the electorate of 'Simcoe. I know Mr. George Chew personally ; with Mr. Manley Chew, so far as I am aware, I am not acquainted. Mr. George Chew is a man of honour, a man of sterling worth, a man who stands high in the business community of north central Ontario ; and I can vouch for it, Mr. Chairman, that When Mr. George Chew gets an opportunity he will be able to settle to his own satisfaction the differences which occur between him and the hon. member for East Simcoe.

This is the old case of too much excuse. I am not complaining that the brother of the hon. member (Mr. Grant* got $50 from Mr. Chew ; Mr. Chew is doing the complaining. He is the gentleman who made the complaint of having been tolled for $50. I do not care whether the hon. gentleman's brother got $100 or not, but I want to know what his brother did for the $50. His name does not appear in the correspondence at all. It is a fortunate thing for Mr. Chew that this gentleman did not write a letter, because if he charges $50 without writing a letter, he would charge $100 if he did write. Some person seems to have done the necessary work, and to have done it with very good results, too.
HUGHE'S. That was for examining the timber.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Grant) states his personal acquaintance with the island, and says that the result of his examination of it was that the timber was worth $200. I care not what the hon. gentleman says personal to myself. I have been in the House some twelve or thirteen years ; I do not know whether I shall be in it any longer or not; but I can say that when I represented East Simcoe and had the patronage of that riding there were never any tolls of $50 taken out of the! pockets of the people. Mr. Chew can cheerfully testify that while I had the patronage of that riding I did many favours for him in the Department of Public Works in reference to the dredging which he required at his mills, and in reference to timber limits in which he was concerned ; but he never had a toll tapper tapping at his pocket for $50. That was unknown in those days. No wonder Mr. Chew bitterly complains that in view of the fact that he was the Liberal candidate in the riding, there is to be a go-between to extract from his pocket $50 before anything could be done. So far as discounting Mr. Chew is concerned. I have only to reiterate that Mr. Chew would
(5249

be very foolish not to accept if any intermediary on behalf of this government should come to him and show him where he could get for $100 $3,000 to $4,000 worth of timber, even if it did cost him $50 for the till-tapper. That is the condition of it. My complaint is not with Mr. Chew or the hon. member for North Ontario.
Or his brother ?

Or his brother either ; he is welcome to the $50 or whatever he got. However that may be, I do complain that the hon. member (Mr. Grant) should have assured the department of his own knowledge of the value of the timber, when he never had been on the island, as he now frankly admits. He had no warrant to state that the timber was only worth $100, and that statement could only have been made with the one idea of deliberately misleading the minister. The inference can be drawn by hon. gentlemen as they please. But the man I am dealing with is this prodigal minister ; this gentleman who is so unsparing with the public domain ; who gives away a steamboat to one party friend and a timber limit to another party friend. I can tell the minister that when it was shown to him that his own official had been cutting the timber he ought to have intervened. No minister will contend that it is right to have this lighthouse keeper acting for the department on the one side and for the contractor on the other. I have nothing to say against Mr. Charles Vallee ; he is a hard working man ; but X will say that l have no doubt that when he was assured that he was to have the contract for cutting the timber, it had some effect on his opinion as to how his report on the value should be. Here is the fact-that while Mr. Vallee was only asked to report as to the cedar and the basswood, he went out of his way to report as to the hemlock and the elm. There was an evident desire on their part to possess themselves of all the timber on this island, while, by the contract, they were confined to the cedar and the basswood. The hon. member for North Ontario says, in his letter of the 13th :
I assure you that great care will be exercised in taking off the soft wood so that no damage will be done to the hard.
Why did he not say that in taking off the cedar and the basswood no harm would be done ? There was a design from the first, and it is shown by the letter of the hon. member for North Ontario, to do, not what was contracted, but to take everything possible, and then to exert the party puli with a pliable minister. The minister would be laughed at around there if he said that he was selling hemlock at $2 a thousand. because it is worth on the stump $6 or $7.

Hemlock to be worth $2 a thousand stumpage must be situated very
close to a sawmill. If I understand the hon. member for North Ontario, this was twenty miles from a sawmill.' I say as a lumberman that hemlock twenty miles from a sawmill is not worth $2 a thousand, and if the Minister of Marine sold it at that price, he sold it for more than it was worth.
I am going, out of the fulness of my heart, to tell the hon. gentleman something. He does not know all about timber.
He knows-
That is my friend who was brought up on cigarettes.
I know what I am talking about when I am talking about cigarettes.

I am going to talk with my timber friend from Richmond and Wolfe. My hon. friend does not know that in our part of the country we take the bark off hemlock trees, and the bark alone is worth $6 a cord. Now, the Minister of Marine knows that it was his duty to expose that lumber for sale and to get the proper price for it. Had those men not been Liberals but Conservatives, they would not have got a foot of that timber. It was a case of a design carefully laid from the beginning to possess themselves of all the timber, and they did so at a very cheap rate. There is not a 'Liberal in the neighbourhood who approves of the transaction. The minister was in fault in this, that when he learned that he had been overreached, that these men were trespassers, and bad taken timber to which they were not entitled under their contract, he should have dealt with them with an iron hand. I congratulate the minister on the way in which he has handled this matter and the sale of the ' Bayfield,' and trust that he will do a little more of the same kind of business in the interest of the Conservative party, though not in the interest of the country.

Agaip I cannot let the statement of the hon. member for East Simcoe pass without a remark from myself. He has not said so in so many words, but be has insinuated, that I myself acted to use a common term, as a till-tapper in approaching the department for Mr. Chew and made some profit. I am therefore under the necessity of stating that during the two years that I have been in Ottawa I have performed services at the various departments, both for Reformers and Conservatives in various parts of the country, and that up to this moment I have never asked, received, nor been promised one cent for my services.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? Did the township of Eldon communicate with him as the Liberal member for North Ontario, and did he not charge them $35 for a little job that

lie had done for them long before he represented that constituency ?
The kon. gentleman refers to an action that I was connected with before I was a member of this House.
I deny that statement emphatically.

The firm that I was connected with in Beaverton, Ontario, Roach & Grant, had to do with an action against the government for damages done by the construction of the Trent Valley Canal; and even if I myself had charged fees, which I did not, I fancy that a solicitor practising in a matter against the government would have every right to charge his clients fees.: However, it did not happen in the case the hon. gentleman has referred to.	[DOT]
I would not have cornered the hon. gentleman, only he was boasting that he had not done so.

I fail to see how I have been cornered. Mr. Chairman, it is a little unpleasant to have to make a personal statement of this sort ; but the hon. member for East Simcoe spoke in a way to make it necessary for me to do so. I do not know what particular advantage a man gets for doing all sorts of work around the departments for people in all parts of the country ; but perhaps I have some of that good nature with which the hon. member for East Simcoe credits the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I may say this, too, that for many of the hon. gentleman's political friends in the east riding of Simcoe I have performed services at the departments and they have written me, apparently not writing to the hon. member for East Simcoe. As my time is fully taken up, I would be very much delighted if they would correspond in regard to such matters with their own member. However, I deem it my simple duty and an act of courtesy which I owe to my fellow citizens, to attend to such departmental matters for them, as may be necessary, and I have done so without expense to them, but with considerable trouble to myself.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
There is a much more serious aspect to this question than has yet been discussed, from my point of view. Not only the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but the entire government, have been entrusted with the care of the property of the people of this country. To-night we have discussed two cases. One case is that of property which belonged to the people of this country in the shape of the steamer ' Bayfield ' which the hon. gentleman made up his mind to dispose of. Did he proceed as an honest man should have done, dealing with property belonging to another-put it up for sale, and have it sold at a fair market value, either by tender or by public auction ? He gets reports from his officers. One Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
report says that the vessel is worth $7,000 ; another says he can get $5,000 cash for her in Goderich ; and yet in the face of that the hon. gentleman hands it over to a political friend for $3,200. Is that the way the country and the people should deal with their property ? Here again we have another case of the timber on 100 acres of land, which formerly belonged to the Indians, but to which these wards of the government relinquished their claims, being sold for a song. The government wanted the timber for lighthouse purposes, but we find the hon. member for North Ontario stepping in and making application for a portion of it. Here is the hon. gentleman's letter :
House of Commons,
Ottawa, August 19th, 1903.
Dear Mr. Prbfontaine,

A constituent of mine is desirous of purchasing the cedar and basswood timber on the lot owned by your department on Hope island in Georgian bay. Your department bought the tract to supply fuel for lighthouse and require only hardwood.
Col. Anderson whom X saw to-day informs me that it is the practice to sell the soft wood and that he recommends the sale provided I arrange price with you.
But if Colonel Anderson, an official of the department, thought it advisable to dispose of part of the wood, why was it not sold at auction ?
My correspondent tells me that the cedar and basswood is sprinkling only and much of it blown down. It rots quickly thus.
Does the hon. gentleman know anything about cedar ? If he does, he would not say that cedar is a timber which quickly rots, On the contrary it is a timber that will hardly ever rot either above or under ground.
He offers $100 for the cedar and basswood, asking that he be allowed two or three years to remove it, at the same time not to damage your hardwood.
Duck island, Col. Anderson tells me, was so disposed of. My own acquaintance with the Hope island convinces me that the price is fair
What is the stumpage under the Ontario government regulations ?
$2 a thousand feet as a rule.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But they sold the limit without calling for tenders.

Mr. Speaker, when the honi member for North Ontario said that basswood would rot, he spoke of basswood! which was blown down, and we are well aware that basswood after it has been blown down and laid on the ground one year, is useless for lumber. Cedar may lie years on the ground without damage; but as regards hemlock being worth $15 a thousand feet, the hon. gentleman knows that he can get at Midland, Ontario, any amount of hemlock at less than $15 a thousand feet. A few weeks ago the Grand Trunk advertised for a lot of hemlock in the Midland* division. The firm with which I am connected tendered at the rate of $12 a thousand feet. The dimension of timber was eight by ten, ten by twelve, twelve by twelve. And we put in a price of $12 a thousand feet. But they li'ad another offer I understood of $11.25 a thousand feet, f. o. b. cars. This timber, I understand, is twenty miles from any saw mill, and it has to be cut down and hauled. I venture to say that hemlock timber at $2 a thousand stumpage is charged all that it is worth. In no place in the province of Quebec, could you get $1 per thousand stumpage at a point twenty miles from n mill. When the hon. gentleman says that there are other hon. gentlemen on the other side who know about the value of fimber and that the member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) knows nothing about it, I take issue with him at once. I do net pretend to know anything about professional matters, but when he says that basswood is worth $30 a thousand feet he has to refer to the hon. member for Addington (Mr. Avery), who tells him that it is worth $25 a thousand. And what percentage of basswood is-worth even $25 a thousand.
Basswood lumber, log run is worth $25 a thousand feet.
The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) said $30.
It is worth more than $30 if you cull it.

But it will not be contended that this timber would average over $25 a thousand. You have only 100 acres of land, twenty miles from a sawmill. If the hon. minister got $100 for the cut basswood and, for the hemlock and elm stumpage charged $2 a thousand, he got a very good price indeed.
What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) think of the prices that the department is paying ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) is aware that there are times in the



year when, if you must have a certain class of timber you must pay the price. The hou. member for Addington (Mr. Avery) is aware that we sell timber at $25 sometimes; that at other times we can get only $10 for. But this is not such a case.

If the lumber expert of bon. gentlemen opposite had desired to be quite fair to the committee he would have told ns-as the fact is-that timber situated as this timber is, on an island in a lake is more easily got to a mill than timber that is only two miles from a mill if you had to haul it over a logging road. And he knows, if he knows anything about timber, that 25 cents a thousand feet would be a large charge for transporting a raft of timber of 200 or 300 thousand, feet to a mill twenty miles away on the shores of a lake.
Oh, oh 1

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) may laugh, but by so doing he betrays either his ignorance of the subject or else a continued effort to deceive the eonw mittee. Every practical lumberman, everyone who has had anything to do with the rafting of timber, knows that conveying timber by water is the very cheapest way. The value of this stumpage would depend entirely upon the situation of the timber. The stumpage would not be worth 25 cents a thousand if the lumber was situated very remote from a place where it could be floated to the mill. If you hauled it ten miles, it might cost so much as to reduce the stumpage to nothing. But, here is timber on an island in the lake, and close to water. Probably it would not have to be put upon a sleigh at all, but simply dragged to the water. In that case $2 or $2.50 a thousand would cut it and haul it to the water. [DOT]
Of course, this timber is located just as the hon. gentleman described it ?
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) undertake to say that it is not ? If it is situated as I have said, it need not be put upon a sleigh
And does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) say that it could be cut and put in the water for $2 a thousand ?
I say $2 a thousand.
Then, he is as much out of the way as my hon. friend from East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett).

I want to tell my hon. friend that I have some acquaintance with the lumber business, that I am interested in lumbering operations quite as large as those in which he is interested. And I know whereof I speak when I say that timber situated as I have suggested can be put into the water at $2 or $2.30 a thousand feet. Of course, as I say, If you have to haul it Mr. TOBIN.
four or five miles before it reaches the water it will cost very much more. It is the hauling by team that is the great expense.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) a question ? Do I understand him to say that he can take a raft of logs and tow it across a lake at 25 cents a thousand feet ?
Fifteen cents.
I said that the timber could be conveyed across the water twenty miles to a mill at 25 cents a thousand feet. If the distance were twenty miles, it could be towed in five or six hours.
I suppose that depends on the wind.
If there is a gale blowing against you, you could not get it out at all. My hon. friend from Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) shows a desire to mislead the committee when he uses such an argument.
I have had experience.

You could not tow a raft at all against a gale of wind. But then you would not attempt it, but would wait until the wind went down. A tow of twenty miles with a raft of 300 thousand feet, which would not require a very big tug to handle, could be made in five or six hours ; and at 25 cents a thousand feet, you would get $75 for the five or six hours work of your tug. I would be glad to be in the tug business if I could get that much for every six hours that my tug worked.
While I am on this subject, I would like to say a word or two with respect to the conduct of the minister and of the department in this matter. We should have been surprised at the conduct of the minister if we had not had an experience with him last session and had never heard of the ' Bayfield ' and the transaction in connection with the sale of, .that steamer. Sale ! I must withdraw that word ; it was not a sale, but a presentation. People have a superstition about a gift of, an edged tool to a friend. So, when one gives a valuable pocket knife costing $5 or $6 to a friend, the friepd gives back a copper cent to take away the harm. So, the hon. minister gave the ' Bayfield ' as a present to his political friends and, to take away the harm they gave him a little sum of money a sum bearing about the same proportion to the value of the ' Bayfield ' as the copper cent does to the five-dollar pocket knife. I say that we should have been surprised at this transaction if we had not had experience of the minister. Let us see how far his conduct is consistent with that of a man who wishes to do his duty to the department. An application was made by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant)-whom, it seems, does not confine his services to his own constituency but extends them all over

his province-for a timber limit on Hope island. And did the minister do as a man would who wished to administer honestly, fairly and properly the department placed in his charge ?
Did he get some expert who knew something about lumber to go over this property and give an estimate of it ? Oh, no, that is not the course the jninister pursued, because that would be the proper course, and it is inconsistent with the hon. gentleman's ideas of public duty to pursue the proper course. So the hon. gentleman takes the letter which he receives from the member for North Ontario, a gentleman who has certainly no expert knowledge of timber, the hon. gentleman who, on a pleasure excursion, sailed by this Oak island, and ventured on the strength of that passing acquaintance to give an estimate, an expert estimate, as to the value of the. timber growing on that island; and he gives the minister to understand that he is thoroughly acquainted with that island, with the conditions and with the timber, and he thinks that $100 is a fair price for the timber to be sold on that application. On the strength of that opinion the minister makes a contract with Mr. Chew for the sale of this timber, which is worth thousands of dollars-basswood and cedar are both very valuable timber, and he has nothing but the opinion of my hon. friend from North Ontario, and an estimate which it seems he has received from the lighthouse keeper. Now this gentleman who may be a very good lighthouse keeper, estimates at $200, as I understand, the value of all the timber on that island, hardwood and softwood. But what do we find as a matter of fact ? We find that after he has taken off the cedar and, the basswood, he has stolen-that is the word, that is the only word to use-what is the use of mincing words in connection with this matter ? Here is a man who makes a hard and fast business contract, a written contract with the department whereby he is to get two certain kinds of timber, basswood and cedar. With that written contract in his hands this mifh goes into the woods and cuts down hemlock to the extent of 140,000 feet, according to the statement of the minister. Now, Sir, if that is not stealing I do not know what stealing means. I say that ' stealing ' is the oniy word you can use in connection with this matter. After this timber thief has stolen 140,000 feet of timber belonging to this country what punishment does the minister inflict upon him ? He charges him a very moderate stumpage; considering the circumstances, considering the situation of this timber, he charges this light fingered gentleman a very moderate stumpage for the timber which he has stolen from the public domain. Now what sort of a position does this minister occupy ? Is this a man who should be entrusted .with the public affairs of this country ? Is this a man who has so slight a regard-the hon. minister laughs

 167J
Yes.

That shows, Mr. Chairman, how slight a regard the minister has for the duties that devolve upon him as the supposedly responsible head of a very important department. Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman imposes on this man the slight tax of $2 per thousand as a punishment. And what does he do with the lighthouse keeper who made this wrong estimate, this lighthouse keeper who, as my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has pointed out, cuts this timber, participates in this fraud, stands up and uses the axe, helps his friend to steal 140,000 feet of timber from the public domain of this country ? He is a man apparently after the minister's own heart, he gets a promotion, no doubt, because he has assisted in defrauding the people of this country out of their rights in connection with this timber. Now this is the man who has induced the department, by the wrongful estimate which he gave, to fall into this error ; and I say, Mr. Chairman, that the minister, if he would even at this late hour recognize his duty, would at once dismiss this man.
He is a good Tory. I will investigate the matter and see what to do.

If he had been a Tory he would have been dismissed long ago. If he had been a Tory he would never have got a chance to participate in this steal. It is only the friends of the hon. gentleman who get a chance to participate in these fat things. Now, Sir, I do think that the minister should have this matter thoroughly investigated and see that the department gets its rights, and if he does that, I am sure the. country will be enriched by a considerable sum.
Rewards for saving life, including life-saving stations, $12,000.
Where are the life-saving stations ?
One at Grand Ma-nan in New Brunswick, and one at Cape Tormentine.
Grand Manan is a large island and there are a good many harbours on it. I would like to know on what part of the island this life-saving station is situated.

I will lay on the table to-morrow a plan of the island and show where the' station is situated.
Investigations into wrecks, $4,000.
How was that expended last year ?

The following investigation took place last year :
' Carrigan Head,' British, stranded six miles from Three Rivers, in April.

' Iberian,' British, stranded near Isle aux Raisins in June.
' Stord,' British, stranded at Ste. Anne des Monts in June, slightly damaged.
' Protector,' Norwegian, Saguenay river, total loss.
' Sardhana,' barque 1,119 tons, British, in July, Point des Monts badly damaged.
' Loughrig Holme,' British, Matane, damage slight.
* Bergenhus,' Norway, St. Charles river, slight damage.
' Monterey,' British, St. Pierre, total loss, two lives.
' Holmlea,' ' Manchester Trader,' ' Mount Royal, 'Rake Manitoba' and ' Topaze.'
While this is very interesting it is not quite the point I want to get at. We want to know how the $4,000 was spent and what officers are employed by the department.

The amount was expended in travelling expenses, fees of witnesses and the holding of the investigations generally. I may state that $4,000 has proved insufficient and I have a further sum of $2,000 in the Supplementary Estimates.
We must have fuller information than that. What officers were employed and what were their salaries ?

Captain Salmon is the officer in charge. He holds the investigations in company with two assessors appointed from time to time by the department from the different localities where the investigations took place. If the hon. gentleman wants the details of the expenditure he will have to give me time to have the books of the department, copied.

In any department the minister should come prepared with all the details in making up the estimates.
Mr. PREFpNTAINE. It may require the copying of a book of 100 pages.
The expenditure of $4,000 could not do that, if you spent it in 5 cent pieces.

In the report of the Auditor General for 1902 we have:
Wrecks reported at $2 each, :-
That is for 1902. We want it for 1903.
The minister 'should have it here.

The hon. gentleman shows that he knows very little how a department is run or even of Mr. PREFONTAINE.
how an office is run. If some one should come to him, if he is a lawyer of any practice, and ask him :	How much do I
owe you ? I have been doing business with you for a year, give me the details at once. He would give the details at once I suppose ?

When the minister asks for $4,000 he has a right to explain to this committee what he did with the money last year, where he expended it, in order that this committee may know whether ic is right for him to have the $4,000 now or not. The minister has been here longer than I and has been a minister for a year and yet does not seem to know che ordinary practice in this House.
Louder.
I want my hon. friend to hear what I have to say. My excitable friend from Victoria generally butts in where he should not. He has worn the hair off his head, butting in.
I want to listen to what the man is saying.

The minister has shown utter ignorance of parliamentary procedure, ignorance which might be excusable in an ordinary member, but which is very inexcusable in a responsible minister. It is the right and duty of the minister to give to the members of this committee the very information for which we are asking, extended up to the end of the last fiscal year and he starts to read to us the expenditure for 1902 instead of 1903.
It is the only one published.

It is not a question of publication. If it were published I would not ask for the information, but the minister has the information in his department and yet the minister says we are not entitled to the information.
I never said anything of the kind. The man puts in my mouth words which I never uttered. He cannot' keep to the truth at all.

I do not know how much more emphatically the minister could say it than by coming here without that information. Why should he come here without the information if he thinks we are entitled to it. If he does not know the procedure he should ask some minister who has been through the mill before. Let him ask the Minister of Fi-nace. The minister is not content with filling the position of his predecessors. He wants' to grab everything in sight and to get the portfolio of public works, and I believe that of canals too. in addition to his own department. Joking aside, the

minister should not ask that this item be passed until he gives us the information we have asked for.
Mr. CASG-RAIN. The Auditor General's Report shows that last year $1,364.45 was expended on this service. The minister now asks $4,000 and promises that he will ask $2,000 more in the supplementary estimates. The committee has a right to know the reason for this increase. The officers of the department do not make out these estimates on mere guess work. They furnish a detailed statement so that more than is required for the public service shall not be asked, and the minister should be in possesion of that detailed statement. We have tried to get explanations from the minister, but the only result is that he insults gentlemen on this side and gets into a passion. What a spectacle it is, and how proud his supporters must feel of this extraordinarily clever minister who has been taken into the cabinet as Minister of Marine and Fisheries, with a large slice of the Public Works Department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I submit to the Minister of Finance, if it is not the duty of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to give this information which to my knowledge every minister has given during the last twenty years.

I have given a list of the investigations which have taken place and the detailed information has never been asked for before as I am informed by the officers of my department-you may laugh as you please. These officials had the confidence of gentlemen opposite for several years ; they have our confidence now and they are not to be laughed at.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The minister has no business saying that. We have not said a word against any of the officials that are on the floor of the House.

I referred to the officials of the department, and stated that they had informed me that this information was never asked for before, when somebody laughed. Some of these gentlemen have been employed in the department for thirty years, and they have given me the formal official information which is usually given in connection with this vote. They state that other information has never been asked for in connection with it. Practically what my hon. friends want is that I shall produce a copy of the ledger with reference to each investigation and I will do that if I get time.
You do not know anything about it.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman says that I do not know what I am talking about.
I rise to a point of order. The minister is putting words into my mouth which I never used.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Even so, it is not a point of order, it is merely a correction.
If the hon. gentleman can show me from ' Hansard ' ever since it has existed that this detailed information with regard to this particular item has been asked for, I stand corrected.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister has not shown how one dollar has been expended out of this $4,000.

The minister has not given one iota of information as to whether these fifteen investigations cost $20 or $200 a piece. We should have that information before this money is voted. The committee desires to be perfectly fair. The minister shakes his head.
I do not dispute it. It is the first time it has been asked.

The minister is entirely out in that statement. Every minister who comes down with his estimates has these details, and I do not see why there should be any exception in the case of the hon. gentleman. We have a right to a detailed statement showing what each investigation cost, how long it lasted, what officials were engaged in it, and what assessors acted in each case. It would take very little time to make up a statement of that sort.	.

Whatever time it will take, the information shall be given. You cannot find that a statement as regards this item has been asked, and the reason I have not got it now is that my officials inform me that it has never been given. But I say I will produce it. What else do hon. gentlemen want ?
If it has not been done heretofore, it has been a great oversight. The idea of voting an item without a word as to how the money has been spent. The information should be here.
It is like many other expenditures which are not given in detail.
But surely the minister ought to have it if it is asked.
If I had expected that it would be asked for, and if I had been informed that it was the practice of the department, I would have had it.

The item should stand
until the information is down.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We asked how much of the $4,000 has been spent last year.
I have said twice -that the total $4,000 has been spent.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We want to know how it has been spent. The Auditor General's Report says that $1,367 was spent last year on investigations into wrecks. How was it spent ? I find the following items : Lucien Bance, clerk in department, travel in connection with investigations at Quebec, $75 ; W. C. Gordon, clerk in department, travelling expenses, $16.40 ; paid for typewriting, $15.75 ; O. G. Y. Spain, travel and disbursements, transport, telephone messages, telegrams, witness fees and expenses, messenger boy and incidental expenses, making a total of $524.85 ; James Swanson, North Sydney, two days, $20 ; Miss Helen Holland, typewriting evidence, $5 ; assessors- R. S. Clift, 11 days, $110 ; expenses, $13.45 ; John Temple,. 11 days, $110; expenses, $15.70 less advance by Mr. Gordon, $25. Now the hon. gentleman comes down and asks for $4,000, and we ask him for infor-' tion, and he refuses to give us the information.
The hon. gentleman should not say I refuse.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes, he absolutely refused to state how he spent the money.
I have stated that I spent more than $4,000 to hold fifteen investigations.

The question is this. M e ask the hon. gentleman for an explanation why this amount is increased, and he says he cannot give the information, and he goes on to state that it is not the practice for any minister to give this information.
I deny it.
