When the hon. gentleman gets into a hole, he denies what he said before. I state that in every other department this is not simply a matter of chance or hazard. The deputy minister or those employed in preparing the estimates, when they go to the minister with them, have to explain every item that makes up the total sum, and if there is an increase, they will have to explain why that increase is made ; and when the minister comes to the House with his estimates, he should be prepared, if he knows what is going on in the department, to state how the money is spent and for what it is needed. Fo!r instance, I see in the 1 Hansard ' reports of last year that the then Minister of Inland Revenue, Mr. Bernier, had all the details at his fingers ends. He knew his business and what he was talking about. Then if we look to the discussions on the estimates of public works, we find the then minister, Mr. Tarte, was never at a loss to give the committee all the information required. Why cannot the hon. gentleman do the same ? Is it possible that he does not know what is going on in his department or can he have lost his memory ? He must have been told what the expenditures were
and what the increases were for, but he will not vouchsafe to take us into his confidence.
I would suggest to the hon. minister that he should let this item stand until he can bring down the details. Let us go on with the next item.

There will be the
same objections.
Mr. FOY/LER. Are we to understand that the hon. minister is not provided with the details of the next item ? Let us then take up some item of which he has'the details.

I know something about the extra costs last year, and I would suggest that as the hon. minister has frankly stated that if you will allow that item to pass, he will bring down the information asked for, you should accede to his request. The iarg; increase over 1902 was made at the. request of the Montreal Board of Trade and the marine underwriters.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why did not the minister say so V

On account of the wrecks in the St. Lawrence, we felt that something had to be done to find out the cause, and appointed men to investigate it. My hon. friend knows some of the men who were appointed. One of them was appointed at my own request, Captain Clift, at $10 a day. No man of his experience would do the work for less money. These gentlemen have sat time and again in the city of Quebec and have gone down to the gulf to make inquiries, and the minister has promised to give us all the details.

If the committee wil! allow me, I would like to make a motion.
I do not know whether it will be in order, and probably I shall be called down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I* move that the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) be appointed Minister of Marine apd Fisheries in place of the present occupant of the position.
Carried.

I think the remarks of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) are very much called for. The increase in this item from 1902, taken in connection with the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that he intends to come down with a supplementary estimate for $2,000. would lead one to suppose that the minister expects more wrecks during the coming season, and requires more money for their investigation. But the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) lias told us that the object is to investigate the cause of these wrecks, so that the department may know what improvements should be made in the aids to navigation with a view to preventing such disasters in the future. But the minister refused all information, and so we had to wait until the hon. member for St. Lawrence spoke. I hope that -the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see the necessity of making reasonable explanations when they are asked for in the committee.

Before the item passes, 1 wish to join with my hon. friends on this side in the praise offered to the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) for the full information he has given us, information that was denied by the minister (Mr. Prefoiltaine). At the same time, I think my hon. friends on this side have been scarcely fair to the minister. It is my desire to be fair to every member of the House, no matter how unfair that member may be to me. And, notwithstanding the fact that the minister has on several occasions to-night spoken in a somewhat testy manner toward myself, yet I wish to offer an explanation of his ignorance on the subject under discussion that, I think, will be satisfactory to the committee. The minister has been very busy of late. There is a gentleman by the name of Oarbonneau who has been having some transactions with the government.
Is that the member of the House ?

No ; but a promoter, of somewhat unsavoury reputation. Mr. Car-bonneau has had negotiations with the government. and these negotiations have been carried on through the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There was also the timber
limit transaction on Hope island, the ' Bayfield ' matter and others of that kind. The minister has been devoting his attention to these things, and matters of detail as to the mere working of his department have escaped his attention. But we are grateful to the understudy of the minister, the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal. We trust that, in the interest of harmony in this House, it will not be long before the coadjutbr of the minister will become minister ; and then, no doubt, we shall be given full details on all subjects.
Expenses and inquiry into the subject of a naval militia and school of navigation, $7,500.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think we have done a good day's work

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that, before we adjourn, we ought to do some business.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We have already done some. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) must admit that the opposition have done no more than discharge their duty by trying to extract a gleam of information from the minister, even though the result has been to gain that information from the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal. By his experience the hon. minister, no doubt, wil! have learned his duty, to give reasonable explanations of expenditures of last year. We want the minister to understand that we must have a little information. I think that, now that all is harmony, now that the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal, has come to the rescue and has given the minister a lesson that, no doubt, he will profit by to the extent of not again attempting to bulldoze the committee, we might close our day's work. We were up late last night, and I think twelve o'clock is late enough for tonight.
I would like to ask the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) if, in his opinion, the hon. member for St. Lawrence division gave a detailed account ?
Does the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Gallery) object ?
No, I only asked the question.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. ynember for St Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) gave the information in quite sufficient detail. He said that the board of trade had recommended a large expenditure for an investigation into the cause of wrecks, and we are ready to accept that.
What had that to do with the statement of the minister ?
Is there to be a scrap between the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Gallery) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) ? Or is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gallery) jealous ?

I am in no way jealous -of tiie lion, member for St. Lawrence. But I thought it fair to say to hon. members, who have so greatly prolonged this debate, that, so far as X could make out, the hon member for St. Lawrence did not give a detailed account. He may have given an account that was accepted as satisfactory by hon. members opposite, but, so far as I could'make out, that account was not given in any detail.

I am sorry if my suggestion that the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Biekerdike) might become a minister has aroused the jealousy of the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Gallery). I dill not know that the hon. member for St. Anne was an aspirant for cabinet honours. I understood that it was a senatorship he was looking for, not a portfolio.

We voted last year $7,500 for this purpose mentioned in this estimate, of which only a certain amount has been expended in preparing diagrams and collecting information for the establishment of a marine school.
Who has charge of this investigation ?
Capt. Salmon.
If I am not mistaken the hon. gentleman told us the same thing last year. Why has nothing more been done 1 What is holding the matter up ?
About $1,800 has been spent in preparing these diagrams.

We were told last year that something was going to be done. I am particularly interested in this matter, because my part of the country is especially Interested in the establishment of a naval school. This is a matter that should be pushed along more rapidly than the minister is pushing it.
If it is the policy of the government to establish a naval militia, I would like to know to what extent the minister has gone, to what extent he has succeeded in establishing a naval militia.

I have just stated that nothing has been done except the preparation of the diagrams, books and so on to organize the department. This sum of $7,500 is a revote, with the exception of $1,800 which has been spent.
I cannot understand what the diagrams have to do with the naval militia.
Diagrams, books and charts have to be prepared to be distributed among the different schools.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The item includes schools of navigation.
Mr. CASG'RAIN.

Nothing has been done about a naval militia except to gather information. After we have inquired into the facts and formed some plan of the organization we propose to make, it will then be time to say what we intend to do. For IJie present we have not made up our minds one way or the other. .
Who is making this preliminary investigation ?

Capt. Salmon. The first thing to do is to prepare for the organization of the schools, and that has been begun. As regards the naval militia, it is a big subject which will entail quite a large expenditure of money, perhaps $500,000 to begin with. Of course, before submitting any plans involving so large an expenditure, we have got to procure all the necessary information, and to do that will take some time.
At whose recommendation has this branch of the service been made ? At whose recommendation has this item of $7,500 for naval militia been put in the estimates ?

The same item was put in last year, and preliminary work was begun. We expect to continue this year, and to come down next year with some plan for establishing the schools, and for the organization of a naval militia.
I am asking at whose recommendation was the item put in here ?

This question has been discussed in the public press for the last two years, and strong representations have been made to the government on the subject. As it is a matter that pertains to the Marine and Fisheries Department, it has been left in my hands and the hands of my officers. Of course we have to go slow, because it will entail so large an expenditure.
My hon. friend has not answered my question yet. At whose recommendation was this item put in, who is the official ?
There are two officials, Capt. Salmon and Capt. Spain.
Was it at their recommendation that this item was put in ?
No, it came from outside, from the Navy League.
Was this item put in by the recommendation of any official in the Marine Department, or is it purely on the initiative of the hon. gentleman himself ?

No. There is in existence a public body called the Navy League, who have made representations to the government on this subject, and we thought proper to put a certain amount in

the estimates to enable us to study the question, first, of naval schools, and then of a naval militia.

The hon. gentleman said there was a discussion in the press. I suppose he referred to the proposition for a Canadian navy. Do I understand that the government have no policy with regard to-that particular matter at the present time ?

We have a policy, that is to say, we have adopted the principle as regards the organization. It is quite a new thing for this country, and we must study it with care before launching it. It is proposed, for instance, that the men employed on the government vessels should form the nucleus of this naval reserve, and that, instead of their being engaged for the season, they should be enrolled for two or three years. As regards the principle of the organization I think the government has entirely made up its mind.
'Mr. KEMP. Then the minister admits that in a country of this size having such a great sea-board we should have a navy of some kind and not be dependent altogether on the navy of Great Britain. We have an immense commerce to protect and should not have to depend oil Great Britain for its protection. It would of course require a large expenditure, but in my opinion the time has come when the government should spend some money on the nucleus of a Canadian navy. The government have been considering this for a numr ber of years and the minister should be able to give us something more definite than he has given.

The item of $7,500 was first put in the estimates last year, and the hon. gentleman remembers how long the session lasted. This might require the despatch of some of my officers to England to get information as to organi-ation, &c., and that has not yet been done, but the first things to provide, I submit, are the schools, and I think that before the end of the session we will be in a position to apnounce that we propose to establish schools in the principal cities of the Dominion.

This is one of the subjects which the ministers discussed in England and this is putting in the thin edge of the wedge some time after they have come back. They do not seem to have any policy except putting in the thin edge of the wedge. $7,500 is a very thin end indeed,' and it is put in to appease some of the gentlemen who have a strong feeling in this matter.
I understand'the minister to say that the government adopt the principle of a naval militia for Canada ?
Yes.

When this naval militia is established and grows to a considerable size will the hon. minister in addition to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Canals and a large share of the Department of Public Wlorks also take over and command this naval militia ? Will that be the intention of the department?'

I do not think the hon. gentleman need worry about that at present.
Some resolutions reported.
FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
Might I ask the hon. the minister what business will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will proceed with Supply, and the estimates of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or of the Postmaster General will be taken up.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: May we expect to have the government Bills, including one with reference to the voters' list, which we were promised on Monday would be brought down on Tuesday or Wednesday ?
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.02 a.m., Wednesday.
Wednesday, June 22, 1904.
